column1: # BacFlux trait genes, version 1 (hand-curated): one row per gene named by trait_rules_v1.tsv, with how it is recognised; ecofolddb keys are Gene@Pathway/Activity names of the EcoFoldDB v2.0 catalogue (Zenodo record 16908168). The columns are explained in docs/analysis/traits.md.

column11: notes

Supporting only. It interconverts the monoene and the diene. In Geobacter metallireducens, the organism its catalogue reference comes from, it dehydrogenates cyclohex-1-ene-1-carbonyl-CoA to the 1,5-diene and so lets cyclohexane carboxylate enter the benzoyl-CoA route (Kung et al. 2014), which means a match marks that route rather than showing an aromatic ring was reduced. No Bakta symbol is listed: the only symbol Bakta gives this family is caiA, a fatty-acid gene.

AcdR is the Lrp-type regulator usually found next to acdS in Proteobacteria (Prigent-Combaret et al. 2008; Nascimento et al. 2014). Its name cannot be told apart from the many other Lrp regulators, so the pattern accepts only an explicit AcdR name. Recognising it by its position next to acdS would need a layer feature. Supporting only.

ACC deaminase and D-cysteine desulfhydrase share one fold, and changing two active-site residues turns one enzyme into the other (Todorovic & Glick 2008). True AcdS has Glu295 and Leu322 (Pseudomonas sp. UW4 numbering, UniProt Q5PWZ8; Nascimento et al. 2014), whereas E. coli D-cysteine desulfhydrase (UniProt P76316) has threonines there. EcoFoldDB's acdS structure (UniProt Q9WY68, Thermotoga maritima, a Swiss-Prot entry named 'putative' and inferred from homology) also has threonines at both positions and is closer to E. coli D-cysteine desulfhydrase (38% identity) than to UW4 AcdS (33%); EcoFoldDB holds the E. coli enzyme too, under sulphur cycling. A structure hit to acdS therefore cannot show ACC deaminase: s_alone is false and the hit only marks agreement. Product names are not used, because Bakta gives the ACC deaminase name, without EC or KO, to desulfhydrase-like proteins; for the same reason Baktfold names cannot count. The symbol 'acd' is not listed because Bakta also gives it to D-cysteine desulfhydrases.

Two things deserve attention. First, the acsA symbol collision is severe - it is the standard symbol for acetyl-CoA synthetase in Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus and Paenibacillus - so the symbol counts only with a matching product and the acetate ligase names are vetoed. Second, the orthologue number is doing all the work, because real achromobactin synthetases carry uninformative product names; that number is shared with staphyloferrin B SbnC, which is why AcsD must be required alongside and why proteins named for staphyloferrin are vetoed. The catalogue entry's accession has been deleted from UniProtKB as a non-reference entry; the archived record shows it is the Dickeya chrysanthemi AcsA, an IucA/IucC-family protein, so the entry is legitimate though uncheckable against a current record. The plain 'achromobactin synthase' is not accepted, because AcsC and AcsD are synthetases of the same cluster.

Not in EcoFoldDB. No orthologue number is used: K23374 covers both this enzyme and the staphyloferrin B synthetase SbnF, and using it would let a baumannoferrin-type or staphyloferrin-type cluster contribute an achromobactin gene line. The acsC symbol collides with the acetyl-CoA decarbonylase/synthase complex subunit gamma in anaerobes, hence the veto and the gating. The staphyloferrin veto stops a synthetase that the annotation names for staphyloferrin (or SbnF) from contributing an achromobactin gene line. It cannot remove every such case, because the annotation itself can name a staphyloferrin synthetase 'Achromobactin biosynthetic protein AcsC'.

Not in EcoFoldDB, and the system-specific gene of this rule: AcsD performs the enantioselective citrate desymmetrisation that starts achromobactin, shown by structures with ATP and citrate and by the reaction with L-serine, and requiring it is what separates achromobactin from staphyloferrin B. The pathway-specific orthologue number (O-citrylserine synthase) is listed; it is shared with PvsD of vibrioferrin, which does not matter because vibrioferrin has nothing matching AcsA or AcsC.

Supporting only. The curated achromobactin pathway module lists four genes (acsD, acsE, acsC, acsA), and this entry lets the audit table show acsE where the annotation names it. The symbol is a trap - in anaerobes acsE is the methyltetrahydrofolate:corrinoid methyltransferase of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, overwhelmingly the commoner meaning - so the symbol is gated and those names vetoed.

The symbol aguA also names alpha-glucuronidase; EcoFoldDB itself has two aguA entries under hemicellulose degradation. So a symbol counts only with a matching name or KO, glucuronidase names are vetoed, and only the putrescine key (UniProt Q8DW17, Streptococcus mutans) is listed. The plain 'N-carbamoylputrescine amidase' name is vetoed, because such proteins can carry the AguA KO; the dual name 'N-carbamoylputrescine amidase / agmatine deiminase' counts here only.

EcoFoldDB's four aguB structures are plant N-carbamoylputrescine amidases (Arabidopsis, tomato, rice, potato). AguB is a nitrilase-family enzyme (Nakada & Itoh 2003), and bacterial amidases and nitrilase-like proteins can best-match these structures with near-equal scores, so structure alone is not enough. Agmatine deiminase names are vetoed, the dual name 'N-carbamoylputrescine amidase / agmatine deiminase' included, because it sits on single proteins that carry the AguA KO.

The same enzyme as PubA of putrebactin, sharing both the orthologue number and the enzyme number with PubA, DesB, BibB and RhbE - the curated orthologue entry lists all of them - so no orthologue or enzyme route is used and only the AlcA names count: the letter name and the Swiss-Prot name 'alcaligin biosynthesis enzyme'. UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the Bordetella bronchiseptica AlcA, a reviewed entry of the lysine/ornithine N-monooxygenase family. Structure alone is not accepted: other proteins, such as a genome's own PvdA, can pass the published thresholds against this entry. The pathway name alone does not count: the regulator AlcR, the exporter Bcr and every other alc protein carry 'alcaligin' in their names too, so one of them would otherwise stand for every gene of the cluster.

Identical in function to PubB of putrebactin; the pathway-specific orthologue number for the alcaligin acyltransferase is listed as a route that does not depend on the word 'alcaligin'. The catalogue entry's accession has been deleted from UniProtKB as a non-reference entry; the archived record shows the Bordetella bronchiseptica AlcB, an MbtK/IucB-like acyltransferase, so the entry is legitimate but unverifiable against a current record. Structure alone is not accepted: acyltransferases of this family are common, so there is no evidence that a structure hit would be specific. Only the letter name AlcB counts by name; the pathway name alone does not, because every protein of the cluster, its regulator and its exporter carry it.

A synthetase of the NRPS-independent siderophore family, so structure alone cannot be allowed: the same fold closes the macrocycle in aerobactin, desferrioxamine, achromobactin, putrebactin and rhizobactin, and UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the Bordetella AlcC with the IucA/IucC domains. The pathway-specific orthologue number for alcaligin synthetase is listed. Only the letter name AlcC counts by name; the pathway name alone does not, because every protein of the cluster, its regulator and its exporter carry it.

The one gene in the alcaligin set with no counterpart in the putrebactin set, which is why the rule requires it, and the curated alcaligin module includes it for the same reason. UniProt shows the catalogue entry is a Bordetella Rieske 2Fe-2S ring-hydroxylating oxygenase, unreviewed and inferred from homology, and the curated orthology calls the step hydroxy-succinyl-putrescine oxygenase; AlcE itself made 2-hydroxyputrescine when it was expressed in Escherichia coli, as did its close paralogue Put2H, which made about three times more (Li et al. 2016); AlcE is also read off one iron-controlled transcript together with the other alc genes. What is still unknown is where it acts: whether alcaligin synthesis starts from free putrescine or from 2-hydroxyputrescine made later. Structure alone is firmly ruled out: other Rieske-type oxygenase components can pass the published thresholds against it. Only the letter name AlcE counts by name; the pathway name alone does not, because every protein of the cluster, its regulator and its exporter carry it.
Supporting only. KEGG gives AnfD the NifD KO, so no KO is used and the iron-only name must be present.

column2: iron-only nitrogenase, delta chain (no counterpart in the molybdenum nitrogenase)
column11: Supporting only; the delta subunit exists only in the alternative nitrogenases.
Supporting only. KEGG files AnfK under the NifK KO, so no KO is used.

Class B non-specific acid phosphatase (AphA, HAD family; Rossolini et al. 1998). A structure hit alone does not count: EcoFoldDB's aphA entries hold a class A PhoN structure (Providencia stuartii) besides class B AphA, and both folds have many non-phosphatase relatives. The symbol aphA also names acetylpolyamine amidohydrolase and aminoglycoside phosphotransferases, so it needs a phosphatase name or KO K03788.

column2: histidine acid phytase (HAP class: E. coli AppA type; also the MINPP type)
column11: Histidine acid phytase class (HAP: E. coli AppA, the Klebsiella phytase, and the MINPP type, which also degrades phytate; Stentz et al. 2014). EcoFoldDB has three HAP structures (E. coli AppA and the fungal PhyA and PhyB) and all three count here: for a bacterial protein the class matters, not which of them is closest. A structure hit alone does not count, because the HAP fold is shared with acid phosphatases that are not phytases; for the same reason the bare name 'histidine acid phosphatase' is not used. The symbol appA also names the oligopeptide-binding protein AppA, so it needs a phytase name or KO. Excluded: Agp ('glucose-1-phosphatase/inositol phosphatase'), which removes only one phosphate from phytate (Cottrill et al. 2002), and 'phytase-like' / 'esterase-like activity of phytase' proteins (Pfam PF13449), a phosphodiesterase-like domain.
Supporting only; it could be recognised only by its position next to ectABC. KO K00928 and EC 2.7.2.4 belong to the housekeeping enzymes and are not used.

Supporting in both anaerobic rules: it marks the activation step that makes benzoyl-CoA, but on its own it is an ordinary adenylate-forming ligase, and the aerobic route through benzoyl-CoA epoxidation uses the same activity. The dual-specificity 4-hydroxybenzoate ligase is vetoed because the catalogue holds it separately as hbaA. bzdA is the symbol for the same ligase in the second class I gene system; that enzyme activates a wider range of aromatic acids than benzoate alone.

Second step of the monoene branch. Its ortholog K07535 is deliberately left out: it holds over a thousand genes and its members are named as general short-chain dehydrogenases, so it would admit ordinary oxidoreductases. No fully specified EC number exists for this reaction.

The ring-cleaving step of the monoene branch, shown to be essential for anaerobic benzoate growth. Two warnings: the catalogue's reference protein is automatically annotated as 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoyl-CoA synthase with EC 4.1.3.36, which is the menaquinone enzyme MenB and not this activity, because the two are close relatives in the crotonase superfamily; and MenB is present in almost every genome. So the EC number and the ortholog are not used, the MenB name is vetoed, and a structure hit never counts alone.

First step of the branch that runs through the monoene, used instead of dch, had and oah by Rhodopseudomonas-type degraders. The same three genes also serve aerobic growth on cyclohexanecarboxylate, so they are only ever asked for together with the four reductase subunits. K07534 is a narrow ortholog and is kept; the fold is a crotonase, so a structure hit never counts alone.

column2: class II benzoyl-CoA reductase, tungsten-containing BamB subunit
column8: benzoyl.?CoA reductase.{0,40}bamB\b|bamB\d?[:/ ].{0,40}(benzoyl.?CoA reductase|aldehyde.?ferredoxin oxidoreductase)|bifurcating benzoyl.?CoA reductase.{0,30}(subunit B)\b
column11: Two problems meet in this gene. Almost every Gram-negative genome has bamB for outer membrane assembly, so the symbol needs a matching product and the assembly-factor name is vetoed. And the subunit itself belongs to the tungsten aldehyde:ferredoxin oxidoreductase family, so plain family members must not count: a structure hit never counts alone, and the plain family name is not matched. The dependable route is the ortholog K19515, which the Bakta database keeps for the real subunits while giving ordinary aldehyde:ferredoxin oxidoreductases the separate K03738. The catalogue holds only the B and C subunits of this eight-subunit complex; several organisms carry more than one bamB copy, so a hit says the complex is present, not which copy is used.

column2: class II benzoyl-CoA reductase, iron-sulfur BamC subunit
column8: benzoyl.?CoA reductase.{0,60}(bamC\b|electron transfer|iron-sulfur)|bamC\d?[:/ ].{0,40}(benzoyl.?CoA reductase|4Fe-4S|ferredoxin)|bifurcating benzoyl.?CoA reductase.{0,30}(subunit C)\b
column11: Same symbol collision as bamB. The electron-transfer subunit is often annotated only as a 4Fe-4S ferredoxin, so the ortholog K19516 carries most of the recognition; the product patterns are written so that a class I subunit name ('benzoyl-CoA reductase subunit B or C') cannot be mistaken for this one.
Supporting. EC 2.3.1.310 is left out because the two thiolase subunits share it. The subunit letter is anchored with a word boundary, so 'subunit B' cannot match the text 'subunit BbsA'.
Supporting. Its KEGG ortholog K07550 is the one the Bakta database keeps most reliably for this gene, so the KO route is what finds the generically named copies.

Supporting, because in several real clusters Bakta names this subunit FabG or beta-ketoacyl-ACP reductase, which no pattern can safely claim. The brackets of the chemical name are escaped so they are read literally, and both 'dehydrogenase' and the abbreviation 'DH' are accepted.
Supporting, for the same reason as bbsC. EC 1.1.1.429 is left out because both subunits share it.

Required: the CoA-transferase is specific to this route and was purified as a two-subunit enzyme, so both subunits are asked for. EC 2.8.3.15 is left out because bbsE and bbsF share it; the KEGG ortholog K07543 is subunit-specific and is kept in the Bakta database, which is what finds copies annotated only as 'CoA transferase'.
Partner of bbsE and required with it, so that one transferred name cannot carry the rule. K07544 is subunit-specific.

A clear case of a transferred name: ordinary acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of aerobic bacteria inherit the BbsG name, and a structure hit then agrees with it, so only the full five-gene set can call the trait. EC 1.3.8.3 is kept because it belongs to this enzyme alone, which is highly specific for the (R) isomer.

Crotonase fold, one of the most promiscuous in this group, so sequence or Baktfold agreement is required. EC 4.2.1.180 is the current number for the reaction; the KEGG module line still shows 4.2.1.128, which belongs to a plant enzyme, so that number is deliberately not used.

column2: class I benzoyl-CoA reductase, subunit A (BadF, BzdQ)
column11: Two gene-name systems describe the same four-subunit enzyme: bcrABCD / badFEDG and bzdQONP. KEGG puts them in the same orthologs, so each subunit entry accepts both. EC 1.3.7.8 is left out of all four subunits because Bakta writes it on each of them. The 4-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA reductase subunits, which the catalogue holds separately as hcrA, hcrB and hcrC, are a different enzyme family and are vetoed by name. Names that say subunit D are vetoed.

column2: class I benzoyl-CoA reductase, subunit B (BadE, BzdO)
column11: Its ortholog K04113 is shared with the 2-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydratase family (2-hydroxyglutaryl- and 2-hydroxyisocaproyl-CoA dehydratase subunits), so the KO alone proves little; this is why the rule asks for all four subunits as two co-localised pairs plus a downstream branch. The KO is still kept because some genomes carry only the generic product name 'Benzoyl-CoA reductase'.

column2: class I benzoyl-CoA reductase, subunit C (BadD, BzdN)
column11: Two unrelated genes carry the symbol bcrC: this reductase subunit and the bacitracin-resistance undecaprenyl-diphosphate phosphatase of Firmicutes and Streptomyces, so the symbol counts only with a matching product and the phosphatase name is vetoed. K04112 is shared with the 2-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydratase family, as for bcrB. The family name 'BcrC/BadD/HgdB' does not count on its own, because it is also given to BcrB and to 2-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydratases; the KO decides.

column2: class I benzoyl-CoA reductase, subunit D (BadG, BzdP)
column11: The ATP-binding subunit. Where Bakta names it only 'CoA-substrate-specific enzyme activase' the KEGG ortholog K04115 is the route that finds it. Names that say alpha or subunit A are vetoed; UniProt calls BcrA the alpha and BcrD the delta subunit.

column2: benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase, large (alpha) subunit; also the TOL plasmid toluate 1,2-dioxygenase alpha subunit XylX
column8: benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase (large|alpha)|benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase subunit alpha|halobenzoate 1,2-dioxygenase large|toluate 1,2-dioxygenase (subunit alpha|large|alpha)|Protein BenA
column11: Reference structure: BenA of Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 (UniProt P07769, Swiss-Prot reviewed). The TOL plasmid toluate dioxygenase XylXYZ is a broad-specificity benzoate dioxygenase that shares common ancestry with BenABC (Harayama et al. 1991), and KEGG gives both one orthology (K05549, benA-xylX), so its names count. EC 1.14.12.10 is left out because Bakta puts it on both the alpha and the beta subunit. Anthranilate, carnitine, biphenyl and phenylpropionate/cinnamate oxygenases share the Rieske fold and are vetoed; a structure hit never counts alone because these multicomponent oxygenases look alike (Neidle et al. 1991).

column2: benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase, small (beta) subunit; also the TOL toluate 1,2-dioxygenase beta subunit XylY
column11: Reference: BenB of A. baylyi ADP1 (P07770, reviewed). KO K05550 (benB-xylY) is specific to the beta subunit and is kept; the shared EC 1.14.12.10 is left out. The beta subunits of these dioxygenases are the less conserved part and probably set the substrate range (Neidle et al. 1991), which is why a structure hit never counts alone.

column2: benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase electron transfer component (ferredoxin and reductase in one protein); also the TOL XylZ
column11: Reference: BenC of A. baylyi ADP1 (P07771, reviewed, evidence at protein level). BenC and XylZ join a plant-type ferredoxin domain to a reductase (Neidle et al. 1991), a common combination, so a structure hit never counts alone.

column2: 1,6-dihydroxycyclohexa-2,4-diene-1-carboxylate (benzoate cis-diol) dehydrogenase; also the TOL XylL
column11: Reference: BenD of A. baylyi ADP1 (P07772, reviewed). Reiner (1971) showed that this NAD-dependent enzyme turns the cis-diol made by the dioxygenase into catechol, and BenD and the TOL XylL belong to the short-chain dehydrogenase family (Neidle et al. 1992), a fold found in every genome, so s_alone is false. KEGG's name for the step (dihydroxycyclohexadiene carboxylate dehydrogenase) is in the pattern too.

column2: choline dehydrogenase (BetA of Gram-negative bacteria; GbsB of Bacillus)
column11: BetA (GMC family) and GbsB (iron-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase family) are unrelated enzymes that catalyse the same reaction, choline to betaine aldehyde (Boch et al. 1996). EcoFoldDB has no BetA structure: its 'betA' entry is the choline oxidase CodA (see codA). Betaine aldehyde dehydrogenase names are vetoed, because such proteins can carry the BetA KO and EC.
Because broad aldehyde dehydrogenases carry this name, the rule requires betB to sit next to betA. Choline dehydrogenase names are vetoed, because some BetA entries carry the BetB EC.

Reference protein UniProt Q53122, reviewed, Rhodococcus jostii RHA1, protein-level evidence. The exclusion guards against a second trap in the catalogue: the pbhA entry is UniProt P17549, the benzoate 4-monooxygenase (cytochrome P450 CYP53A1) of the fungus Aspergillus niger, whose protein name is given as 'Benzoate 4-monooxygenase bphA'. No bph gene lists hcaE as a symbol. KO K08689 is gene-level but KEGG also maps it to dioxin degradation, which is the same enzyme acting on another substrate.

Reference protein UniProt Q53123, reviewed, R. jostii RHA1. No EC listed: 1.14.12.18 is shared with the ethylbenzene dioxygenase subunits, which the catalogue also holds. The alpha and beta subunits of this family are paralogues of one ancient duplication, so they look alike to a structure search.

Reference protein UniProt Q53124, reviewed, R. jostii RHA1. A Rieske [2Fe-2S] ferredoxin; this component and the reductase were acquired from unrelated oxygenase systems, so neither names a substrate on its own. The look-ahead keeps the ferredoxin pattern from matching the ferredoxin reductase name.

Reference protein UniProt Q0S032, reviewed, R. jostii RHA1. A flavin reductase outside its cluster context, so s_alone is false. It is inside the oxygenase co-localisation group: in the Gram-positive degrader RHA1 the four components are consecutive, and in the Gram-negative degraders the reductase gene sits two genes further along, after the dehydrogenase and the ring-cleavage gene, which a chain of up to ten genes accommodates.

A short-chain dehydrogenase, so structure alone is not enough. The catalogue's reference protein for this key, UniProt A0A097SRI2, is a TrEMBL entry for Cupriavidus sp. WS whose product was characterised by expression in Escherichia coli, where it dehydrogenated the dioxygenase's dihydrodiol product (Wang et al. 2015). UniProt has deleted the accession because that proteome is not a reference proteome, so the structure stays usable but the record cannot be looked up.

The ring-fission product of this enzyme is the compound the plate assay in the rule looks for. An extradiol ring-cleavage enzyme of the same class as the catechol 2,3-dioxygenase, so sequence agreement is required. The catalogue's reference protein, UniProt A0A097SRG2, is a TrEMBL entry for Cupriavidus sp. WS whose product was characterised by expression in Escherichia coli, where it cleaved the ring of 2,3-dihydroxydiphenyl ether (Wang et al. 2015). UniProt has deleted the accession because that proteome is not a reference proteome, so the structure stays usable but the record cannot be looked up.

Reference protein UniProt Q75WN8, unreviewed, R. jostii RHA1 bphD1, with protein-level evidence. The pattern also accepts the KEGG wording '2,6-dioxo-6-phenylhexa-3-enoate hydrolase' and the 'dienoic acid' spelling, because Bakta uses both. Second textbook case for s_alone false, this time the alpha/beta hydrolase fold; ExPASy also notes that this enzyme cleaves the ring-fission products of 3-isopropylcatechol and 3-methylcatechol, so it is not specific to biphenyl. The characterised Gram-positive biphenyl cluster does not contain this gene at all (Masai et al. 1995), which is why it is not in any co-localisation group.

One token for two catalogue entries. The entry labelled bphH in 'catechol degradation' is in fact TesE of Comamonas testosteroni (Q83VZ5, reviewed, evidence at protein level), the 2-hydroxyhexa-2,4-dienoate hydratase of testosterone breakdown; the mhpD entry is the E. coli phenylpropionate-pathway hydratase (P77608, reviewed). KEGG puts BphH, XylJ and TesE in one orthology (K18364, 2-oxopent-4-enoate/cis-2-oxohex-4-enoate hydratase) beside MhpD (K02554), so both count as this step. The names are genuinely shared, so any strain with a phenylpropionate lower pathway finds this gene; that is why the catechol rule demands the ring-cleavage dioxygenase in the same chain. Generic fumarylacetoacetate-hydrolase names are vetoed so they cannot double as dmpH. Decarboxylase names are vetoed for the same reason: names and KOs of the two enzymes are often swapped. The family name 'hydratase/decarboxylase' does not trigger the veto: it names neither step, so the KO and EC decide.

Two catalogue references for one step: BphI of Paraburkholderia xenovorans LB400 (P51015, reviewed, biphenyl pathway) and MhpE of E. coli (P51020, reviewed, phenylpropionate pathway). KO K01666 and EC 4.1.3.39 are not used, because Bakta also puts them on a conserved protein named 'Pyruvate carboxyltransferase' that has nothing to do with these pathways, while every real meta-pathway aldolase is recognised by its name (and K18365 is kept). Like bphH, this step is shared with the phenylpropionate and other meta pathways, so finding it alone means little.
SAM-dependent methyltransferases form a huge family, so a structure hit alone is not counted (Waditee et al. 2003; Nyyssölä et al. 2000).
As for bsmA: a structure hit alone is not counted.

column2: benzylsuccinate synthase, alpha subunit (glycyl radical enzyme)
column8: benzylsuccinate synthase.{0,25}(alpha|subunit A)\b|alpha.?subunit of benzylsuccinate synthase|bssA[:/ ].{0,30}benzylsuccinate synthase
column11: The alpha subunit carries the glycyl radical. The same family holds pyruvate formate-lyase, which nearly every anaerobe has, and the fumarate-adding enzymes for n-alkanes and 2-methylnaphthalene, so those product names are vetoed and a structure hit never counts on its own. The subunit word is required because Bakta gives the plain name 'benzylsuccinate synthase' to the beta and gamma subunits as well, and EC 4.1.99.11 is left out for the same reason: Bakta writes it on all three subunits. Where Bakta falls back to 'Glycyl radical enzyme' the gene is missed, which is one reason the rule also asks for four bbs genes.

column8: benzylsuccinate synthase.{0,25}(beta|subunit B)\b|beta.?subunit of benzylsuccinate synthase|\bbssB\b
column11: Not in the catalogue, so this gene can only come from Bakta's or Baktfold's name. Supporting, because Bakta sometimes names this small subunit generically (for example as an activating enzyme), which would cost a call if it were required. Its KEGG ortholog K29040 is specific to the beta subunit.

column8: benzylsuccinate synthase.{0,25}(gamma|subunit C)\b|gamma.?subunit of benzylsuccinate synthase|\bbssC\b
column11: Not in the catalogue, so Bakta or Baktfold names only. Supporting for the same reason as bssB. K29041 is specific to the gamma subunit.

The family is also named 'Saccharopine dehydrogenase', which is too broad to match, so structure evidence matters for this gene; EcoFoldDB's background holds fungal saccharopine dehydrogenases and a lysine dehydrogenase, against which a cansdh hit must win. The related carboxyaminopropylagmatine dehydrogenase (CAPADH; KO K27502, EC 1.5.1.55) uses agmatine instead of putrescine and also leads to spermidine (Xi et al. 2023); Bakta's names and EcoFoldDB do not separate the two, so both count. The genes need not sit next to nspC: they are adjacent in Vibrio cholerae (Lee et al. 2009) but far apart in Campylobacter jejuni and Helicobacter pylori, where the pair carries the CAPA orthologue numbers and the route still ends in spermidine (Hanfrey et al. 2011; Xi et al. 2023). Decarboxylase names are vetoed, because carboxynorspermidine decarboxylases can carry this enzyme's KO and EC.

Reference: CatA of A. baylyi ADP1 (P07773, reviewed, evidence at protein level). symbol_needs_product is true because catA is also the type A chloramphenicol acetyltransferase. A structure hit may count alone because the look-alikes either fail the coverage filter (the protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenase chains are 201 and 241 residues against 311 for CatA) or are catalogue entries themselves (both protocatechuate dioxygenase chains and hydroxyquinol 1,2-dioxygenase), so the best hit chooses between named enzymes. Chlorocatechol 1,2-dioxygenases of the modified ortho pathway have a name that contains the catA name and are vetoed: that pathway descends from the catechol branch but is a separate route without muconolactone isomerase (Harwood & Parales 1996). Generic 'intradiol ring-cleavage dioxygenase' names are not vetoed, so a structure hit can still rescue a real enzyme with a vague name.

Reference: muconate cycloisomerase I of Pseudomonas putida (P08310, reviewed, evidence at protein level). The name pattern is deliberately loose, because some real catB carry only the family name; that is safe only because the rule demands catA and catC in the same chain. Enolase-superfamily enzymes such as glucarate, galactarate, galactonate and rhamnonate dehydratases are close in structure to this reference and are kept out only by better hits to non-catalogue structures, so a structure hit needs the name to agree. The exact name 'Mandelate racemase' is accepted, because Bakta gives that name to actinobacterial CatB such as the cis,cis-muconate cycloisomerase of Arthrobacter sp. BA-5-17, whose genes are clustered catRBCA (Murakami et al. 2004). It is anchored to the whole product name, and because it counts only inside a chain with catA and catC, and a partial of the rule needs catC, the galactonate dehydratases that share the name can carry neither a call nor a partial. Chloromuconate cycloisomerases (modified ortho pathway) are vetoed for the same reason as chlorocatechol dioxygenases in catA. Bakta usually gives this gene the symbol rspA, not catB.

Reference: CatC of Cupriavidus pinatubonensis JMP134 (P80573, reviewed, evidence at protein level). A small (92-residue), distinctive protein and the only member of its family in the catalogue, with no known look-alike that scores strongly, so a structure hit counts alone. Muconolactone isomerase is also the step that tells this branch from the chlorocatechol (modified ortho) pathway, which has no such enzyme, so this is the gene a partial of the rule needs. Proteins named only 'Muconolactone isomerase domain-containing' are vetoed, because they sit outside cat clusters, whereas the characterised CatC belong to UniRef90 clusters named after the enzyme itself. The carboxymuconolactone decarboxylases of the protocatechuate branch are vetoed too. Racemase names are vetoed too, because a 'mandelate racemase' entry can carry the CatC EC.

column2: choline oxidase (CodA; oxidises choline to glycine betaine by itself)
column11: EcoFoldDB's 'betA' structure is the Arthrobacter globiformis choline oxidase (UniProt Q7X2H8, gene codA), which performs both oxidation steps (Fan et al. 2004), so that key is mapped here; KEGG module M00555 also accepts choline oxidase alone. GMC oxidoreductases form a large family, so a structure hit alone is not counted. In Arthrobacter pascens choline oxidase is a catabolic enzyme under catabolite repression, and glycine betaine is used there as a carbon source rather than as an osmolyte, although the cloned gene protects Escherichia coli against salt (Rozwadowski et al. 1991).

column2: ent-copalyl diphosphate synthase (class II diterpene cyclase of the gibberellin operon)
column11: Bakta names the rhizobial CPS after its Swiss-Prot entry from Sinorhizobium fredii NGR234, 'Uncharacterized protein y4kT' (UniProt P55538, 516 aa); the pattern matches that name and must follow if UniProt renames the entry. EcoFoldDB's cps structure (UniProt Q5KSN5) is a bacterial ent-CPS, but from a Streptomyces viguiepinol cluster, not a gibberellin operon. A structure hit counts alone, but on its own it only means a class II diterpene cyclase, which is why the rule needs the whole operon. 'Copalyl diphosphate synthase' without 'ent-' is not matched, because Streptomyces use that name for normal-CPP synthases of other diterpenes. The symbol cps is not used because capsule genes share it.

column2: cytochrome P450 CYP112 (GA 20-oxidase, GA12 to GA9)
column11: CYP112 makes GA9 from GA12, the last step of the operon pathway (Nett et al. 2017).

column2: cytochrome P450 CYP114 (ent-kaurenoic acid oxidase; works with the operon ferredoxin)
column11: In some rhizobia the operon's ferredoxin gene is fused in frame with cyp114 (a mostly Rhizobium clade) or with the SDR gene (a mostly Mesorhizobium clade) (Nett et al. 2020). Bakta can misname CYP114, for example as 'Ferredoxin'; its KO K21117 still counts it. EcoFoldDB's ent-kaurenoic acid oxidase structures (kao) are plant CYP88 enzymes and are not used.

column2: cytochrome P450 CYP115 (gibberellin 3-oxidase, GA9 to bioactive GA4)
column11: Present in the operons of plant pathogens and of a few rhizobia; it turns GA9 into bioactive GA4 (Nett et al. 2017, ACS Chem Biol). In Mesorhizobium loti it lies away from the rest of the operon (Nett et al. 2020). Supporting only, but it marks strains that can make GA4 themselves. KEGG has no KO for CYP115.

column2: cytochrome P450 CYP117 (ent-kaurene oxidase of the gibberellin operon)
column11: Bakta uses the original Bradyrhizobium names: P450 BJ-4 is CYP117, BJ-3 is CYP114 and BJ-1 is CYP112, as the KOs and symbols Bakta attaches to them confirm. CYP117 oxidises ent-kaurene to ent-kaurenoic acid (Nett et al. 2017). EcoFoldDB's ent-kaurene oxidase structures (ko) are plant CYP701 enzymes that any bacterial P450 resembles, so they are not used.

The ortholog K07537 is the safety net for genomes where Bakta writes only 'enoyl-CoA hydratase' or 'Crotonase', and it is specific in practice, because Bakta keeps it for the real enzyme and does not hand it to ordinary crotonases. The catalogue's reference protein for this entry is an unreviewed protein named only 'enoyl-CoA hydratase', which is exactly why a structure hit cannot count on its own; it sits next to the following two genes in its genome, which is what supports the assignment. Bakta can name the enzyme only by its other official name, 'Dienoyl-CoA hydratase' (an alternative name of EC 4.2.1.100 in ExPASy ENZYME), with no KO, as in Aromatoleum aromaticum EbN1; that name counts only at the start of the product, so names such as '2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase' cannot match.

The generic lysine decarboxylase enzyme number and orthologue (the housekeeping CadA and LdcC every enterobacterium carries) are deliberately not used; either route would find this gene in a large share of all genomes. What is used instead is the pathway-specific orthologue number that the curated orthology gives the desferrioxamine and bisucaberin decarboxylase, plus the DesA and DfoJ name forms. The dfoJ symbol is accepted because in Erwinia and Pantoea the desferrioxamine E genes are dfoJ, dfoA and dfoC, and the DfoJ structure has been solved as the pathway's lysine decarboxylase. The desaturase veto is needed because a fatty-acid desaturase can also carry the DesA name, as in 'Delta-9 fatty acid desaturase, DesA'. Structure alone is not accepted: the catalogue entry is a pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase fold, and other pyridoxal-dependent enzymes, such as threonine aldolases and class V aminotransferases, can pass the thresholds against it. The entry itself is weakly provenanced - an unreviewed Streptomyces 'Pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase', inferred from homology, with no desferrioxamine annotation - so it is treated as family-level.

The catalogue entry for this gene is a Streptomyces protein UniProt calls 'L-lysine N6-monooxygenase MbtG', which is why the mbtG symbol and name forms are accepted - and that is not guesswork about an odd label: the same protein was purified, crystallised and shown to be a broadly specific cadaverine N-hydroxylase of the desferrioxamine B pathway. The dfoA symbol is accepted for the Erwinia and Pantoea form of the pathway. The orthologue number is the one shared across alcA, pubA, desB, bibB and rhbE, kept deliberately as a family-level route while the rule guarantees the gene can never call anything alone. No enzyme number is listed. EC 1.14.13.59, L-lysine N6-monooxygenase, is the number of the aerobactin enzyme IucD, whereas DesB is a cadaverine N-hydroxylase whose number is only EC 1.14.13.-, so the lysine-specific number is not used; the putrescine N-hydroxylase number that some annotations give this protein is shared with AlcA and PubA and is left out as well, so an alcaligin or putrebactin hydroxylase is not counted as desB. Acyltransferase names are vetoed: Bakta's database gives this orthologue number to an N-acyltransferase joined to a siderophore synthetase ('Lysine N-acyltransferase MbtK'), which has no hydroxylase domain.

Not in EcoFoldDB, so sequence names and the pathway-specific orthologue number only. The acyltransferases of the hydroxamate siderophore pathways are one family and the annotation names them MbtK or IucB-like rather than DesC, which is why those forms are accepted; the price is that an aerobactin cluster also matches here. The symbol is gated because desC is the stearoyl-CoA desaturase symbol in several actinobacteria. The dfoC forms are accepted because in Erwinia and Pantoea this activity and the synthetase activity of desD are fused into one protein whose structure shows an acyltransferase domain joined to an NRPS-independent siderophore domain: in such a genome one protein satisfies both desC and desD, deliberately. The pattern avoids the bare 'GNAT family N-acetyltransferase', one of the commonest annotations there is. 'Desferrioxamine ... biosynthesis protein' counts only with the letter name DesC, because the DesA, DesB and DesD names start the same way.

column8: IucA/IucC family siderophore|aerobactin synth(ase|etase)|desferrioxamine (E )?synth|6-N-acetyl-6-N-hydroxy-L-lysine ligase|desferrioxamine.{0,40}\bDesD\b|\bDfoC\b|siderophore biosynthesis protein,? (IucA/IucC family|Iuc[AC]\b)
column11: The pattern is openly family-level, because the family cannot be split by name or by fold: the same enzyme class closes the macrocycle in desferrioxamine, aerobactin, achromobactin, alcaligin, putrebactin and rhizobactin, and the annotation can call a genuine Streptomyces desferrioxamine synthetase 'Aerobactin synthase', the same name real aerobactin synthetases carry. The pathway-specific orthologue number is listed as the one precise route. Co-localisation with desA, desB and desC is what makes the call, and an aerobactin-positive strain still finds this gene, which is why the rule asks for desA before reporting a partial: without the decarboxylase, such a strain is not called. The receptor and binding-protein vetoes keep uptake proteins out, since they often carry the siderophore's name. 'Desferrioxamine ... biosynthesis protein' counts only with the letter name DesD, and 'siderophore biosynthesis protein' only with IucA/IucC in the name: on its own it also names many lysine and ornithine N-hydroxylases, the desB step.

Supporting only, which is just as well: the annotation can use the dhbA symbol for entA inside an enterobactin cluster, as in Salmonella, so this token cannot be read as proof of bacillibactin. It scores one gene of a five-gene picture there, far short of a call.

Supporting only. The orthologue number for this step is the one shared with EntB, VibB and MxcF, and is used on the entB token rather than here, so that one protein is not counted twice under two different system names.

Narrow for the same reason as dhbE: plain 'isochorismate synthase' is the menaquinone enzyme MenF in nearly every genome, and Bacillus subtilis carries duplicate isochorismate synthases, one for menaquinone and this one for dihydroxybenzoate. Not in EcoFoldDB.

Deliberately narrow, and the narrowness is the point. The enzyme is identical to EntE of enterobactin and shares its product name and orthologue number, so a pattern built on the enzyme description would make every enterobactin producer look like a partial bacillibactin producer. Restricting the token to the dhbE symbol and name form avoids that, at the cost of missing bacillibactin where the annotation gives this gene no symbol - a real limitation.

The protein is dimodular, not trimodular: the primary paper re-sequenced dhbF, corrected the published annotation and showed it activates threonine and, less efficiently, glycine, and UniProt's reviewed entry names it a dimodular non-ribosomal peptide synthase. Only the glycine-ligase enzyme number is used; the threonine-ligase number it also carries is shared with the pseudomonine synthetase PmsD. Structure alone is not accepted, for the strongest reason in the group: large NRPS proteins of other systems can pass the published thresholds against this entry, and a protein that survives the best-hit filter can score identically against this entry, the mycobactin mbtE entry and a third catalogue structure.

Two catalogue references for one reaction (EC 1.13.11.2): DmpB of the phenol-degrading Pseudomonas sp. CF600 (P17262, reviewed) and CatE (YfiE) of Bacillus subtilis (P54721, reviewed, evidence at protein level). They are different proteins (KEGG K00446 and K07104), and CatE is a protective enzyme: B. subtilis needs it to survive catechol but cannot grow on catechol (Tam et al. 2006), the clearest reason why this dioxygenase alone is never a trait. A structure hit may count alone because one-domain extradiol proteins fail the coverage filter and the two-domain look-alikes (4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, 2,3-dihydroxybiphenyl dioxygenase BphC, the p-cumate enzyme CmtC, HpaD, PhdF) are catalogue entries, so the best hit chooses between them (extradiol dioxygenase families: Eltis & Bolin 1996); the choice can be close, so the substrate is a lead. Only names of other specific enzymes are vetoed; generic VOC or glyoxalase family names are not, so a structure hit can still rescue a real enzyme with a vague name. Bakta hands the symbol catE to glyoxalase and VOC family proteins, hence symbol_needs_product.

Reference: DmpC of Pseudomonas sp. CF600 (P19059, reviewed). KEGG K10217 covers both 2-hydroxymuconate-6-semialdehyde and 2-aminomuconate-6-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (EC 1.2.1.85 and 1.2.1.32) and also PraB of protocatechuate 2,3-cleavage (Kasai et al. 2009); bacterial tryptophan breakdown runs through 2-aminomuconate and 4-oxalocrotonate (Colabroy & Begley 2005). These enzymes cannot be told apart by name, one reason the rule needs the catechol 2,3-dioxygenase in the same chain. Aldehyde dehydrogenase fold, so s_alone is false. The veto keeps every homoprotocatechuate degrader from gaining a false dmpC.

Reference: DmpD of Pseudomonas sp. CF600 (P19076, reviewed). The 2-hydroxy-6-oxohepta-2,4-dienoate name is the same hydrolase acting on the 3-methylcatechol product. Bakta's symbol xylF is the TOL name for this gene but also the xylose ABC binding protein, so the symbol only counts with a matching product. Alpha/beta hydrolase fold, so s_alone is false.

Reference: XylI of the TOL plasmid (P49155, reviewed, evidence at protein level), which works in a complex with the hydratase (MetaCyc pathway PWY-5420). dmpH and bphH are both fumarylacetoacetate-hydrolase-fold proteins, so the generic family name is left to the KO route here and vetoed in bphH, to keep the two steps apart. Hydratase names are vetoed here: names and KOs of the two enzymes are often swapped, and a name that offers both ('... decarboxylase/... hydratase') counts for neither. The family name 'hydratase/decarboxylase' does not trigger the veto: it names neither step, so the KO and EC decide.

Reference protein UniProt P19729, reviewed, Pseudomonas sp. CF600, protein-level evidence; its alternative names include 'Phenol hydroxylase P0 protein', so the P0/A0 wording is accepted. DmpK is not part of the catalytic complex: it is needed to assemble the active oxygenase, which is made inactive without it and can then be activated with ferrous iron only in DmpK's presence. Alternative symbols are the Pseudomonas phl and the Acinetobacter mph genes; the symbol mop is not accepted, because no phenol hydroxylase gene of that name exists in UniProt. The ubiquinone polyprenylphenol hydroxylases are vetoed in every phenol hydroxylase entry (dmpK to dmpP), because their names often contain the word phenol (2-octaprenylphenol hydroxylase, say); 'propane' is vetoed because the same dmp and mph symbols are also given to propane 2-monooxygenases.

Reference protein UniProt P19730, reviewed, CF600, protein-level evidence, alternative name 'Phenol hydroxylase P1 protein'. The P0 to P5 and A0 to A5 alternative names are kept because they are still in use for these operons, including for the Acinetobacter mph system.

Reference protein UniProt P19731, reviewed, CF600. A small activator protein that is required for activity in vitro, so it belongs in the required set, but its fold is too small and too common for a structure match to name it.

column2: phenol 2-monooxygenase, catalytic oxygenase component DmpN (diiron active site)
column11: Reference protein UniProt P19732, reviewed, CF600, protein-level evidence. This is the catalytic diiron subunit, the one that resembles the methane, toluene and alkene monooxygenases of the same soluble diiron family, so structure alone must not name it. The 'large subunit' and 'alpha subunit' wordings are accepted because UniProt uses them for dmpN homologues. EC 1.14.13.244 is left out because it is written on the other components too (DmpL, DmpM, DmpO and DmpP), and names that carry another Dmp letter are vetoed.
Reference protein UniProt P19733, reviewed, CF600. Named only by its subunit letter in most databases, which is why the pattern keys on 'component ...O' and on the P4/A4 wording.

Reference protein UniProt P19734, reviewed, CF600. A flavin and iron-sulfur reductase, the least specific component of the complex: this fold is shared with the electron-transfer components of unrelated oxygenase systems, so it depends on the name.
EctA is a small GNAT acetyltransferase. A structure hit alone is not counted, so that a stray hit plus a diaminobutyrate aminotransferase elsewhere cannot produce a 'partial' call.

ectB counts only inside a co-localised ectA-ectB-ectC chain. One of EcoFoldDB's two ectB structures (UniProt E1V7V7, Halomonas elongata) is DoeD of the ectoine-degradation pathway (Schwibbert et al. 2011), so structure hits to this key also come from ectoine breakdown; s_alone is false. KO K00836 is shared with the siderophore enzymes RhbA and PvdH. EC 2.6.1.76 is shared with those and with DoeD (KO K15785). Neither is used.
EctC is a small cupin-fold protein. Cupins are widespread, so a structure hit alone is not counted.
Supporting only (Bursy et al. 2007). Not in EcoFoldDB's catalogue.

Supporting only, and not in EcoFoldDB. The symbol is gated by the product because Enterococcus uses entA for an unrelated bacteriocin whose product is simply 'EntA'. Matching the bacillibactin dhbA and the fabG-named paralogues is expected and intended: this is the shared catecholate pathway, which is why it is supporting and never required.

Supporting only. The orthologue number is shared with DhbB, VibB and MxcF - the curated orthologue entry names all four - and is kept because it is the one route that finds this gene where the annotation leaves it as a bare 'isochorismatase'. The exclusions remove the YcaC-like isochorismatase-family cysteine hydrolases and secreted isochorismatase effectors, a different activity on the same fold.

Supporting only. The exclusions matter more than the inclusions: isochorismate synthase is also the first step of menaquinone synthesis (MenF, a separate orthologue present in nearly every genome) and of salicylate synthesis (PchA, MbtI, YbtS), so those names are vetoed. Without them this token would match a large share of all genomes.

The orthologue number and the enzyme number for this step are shared with DhbE of bacillibactin, VibE of vibriobactin and MxcE of myxochelin, so neither is used; only the enterobactin-specific name forms and the entE symbol count. That is what keeps a Bacillus bacillibactin cluster from being reported as a partial enterobactin producer. Structure alone is not accepted: unrelated acyl-CoA and long-chain fatty-acid ligases can pass the thresholds against this entry. Bakta also gives the entE symbol to related adenylation enzymes of other siderophores, such as MbtA of mycobactin, so a lone entE is not evidence of enterobactin: entF is the rule's key gene, and without it no partial is reported.

column8: entero(bactin|chelin) (synthase|synthetase) (subunit|component) F(?![A-Za-z])|entero(bactin|chelin) non-ribosomal peptide synthetase|^entero(bactin|chelin) synthase multienzyme
column11: The pattern names the synthetase specifically, because the siderophore's name appears in every transporter, receptor and esterase name of the cluster; the older name 'enterochelin' is accepted too. A second trap: the plain pattern 'subunit E' is a prefix of 'subunit EntD', so the trailing guard stops entE and entF matching EntD. The 'enterocin' veto is insurance against bacteriocin products, but an Enterococcus protein whose product is just 'EntF' is kept out by the symbol gating, not by that veto. Only the serine-ligase enzyme number is used; 6.3.2.14 is shared with entB, entD and entE in real annotations. Structure alone is not accepted: large carrier-domain proteins of other systems can pass the thresholds against this entry. The 'enterobactin synthase multienzyme' wording counts only at the start of the name, as in EntF's name; the EntD and EntE names end with '... component of enterobactin synthase multienzyme complex'.

column2: glutamate decarboxylase (GadA/GadB of E. coli, GadB of lactic acid bacteria)
column11: One token covers EcoFoldDB's gadA and gadB structures (UniProt P69908, P69910): the two E. coli paralogues are 99% identical (5 differences in 466 residues), so separate tokens would report every hit twice and flag it as a near-tie. EcoFoldDB's background holds other group II decarboxylases (histidine, tyrosine, aromatic-L-amino-acid and diaminobutyrate decarboxylases), so a best hit to gad counts alone; the borderline flag marks near-ties.

GadC (EcoFoldDB: Lactococcus lactis, UniProt O30417) is an APC-family antiporter. EcoFoldDB's background lacks most APC permeases, so putrescine-ornithine, arginine-ornithine and ethanolamine permeases can best-match its structure: structure alone is not enough. Supporting only.

column2: gluconate 2-dehydrogenase (membrane-bound, makes 2-ketogluconic acid from gluconic acid; any of its three subunits)
column11: Supporting: membrane-bound gluconate 2-dehydrogenase (flavoprotein, cytochrome c and small subunit) that oxidises gluconic acid further to 2-ketogluconic acid; any subunit counts. Called gad by de Werra et al. (2009) and written gadh here because gad is the glutamate decarboxylase token; no Bakta symbol is used because Bakta puts the symbols betA and cccA on these proteins. Excluded: phosphogluconate dehydrogenases and a glucoside 3-dehydrogenase that Bakta names 'Gluconate 2-dehydrogenase, family AAnc'.

Reference: GalD of P. putida KT2440 (Q88JY0, reviewed, evidence at protein level), the 4-oxalomesaconate tautomerase of gallate breakdown (Nogales et al. 2011); the catalogue files it under protocatechuate degradation because the gallate and protocatechuate 4,5-cleavage routes share this step. The protocatechuate route's own enzymes (LigU in Sphingobium, PmdU in Comamonas) belong to the same PrpF family (Hogancamp & Raushel 2018) and the step is essential (Kamimura et al. 2010), but the family name also sits on methylcitrate-cycle and unknown-function paralogs, so this gene is supporting only and never counts from structure alone.

column2: membrane-bound PQQ-dependent glucose dehydrogenase (makes gluconic acid in the periplasm)
column8: quinoprotein glucose dehydrogenase( A)?$|membrane-bound (PQQ-dependent |quinoprotein )?glucose dehydrogenase|PQQ-dependent glucose dehydrogenase|glucose/quinate/shikimate family
column11: Membrane-bound PQQ glucose dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.5.2): oxidises glucose to gluconic acid in the periplasm, the main route by which Gram-negative bacteria dissolve calcium phosphates. Accepted names include NCBI's family name 'membrane-bound PQQ-dependent dehydrogenase, glucose/quinate/shikimate family', which also covers quinate dehydrogenase (QuiA), so a gcd line resting only on that name is weaker. Excluded: soluble glucose dehydrogenase B (GdhB, a different PQQ enzyme, EC 1.1.99.35), soluble PQQ 'sugar dehydrogenases', and NAD(P)-dependent 'glucose 1-dehydrogenase' (for example Bacillus Gdh). E. coli and Salmonella carry gcd but make no PQQ (Hommes et al. 1984; Liu et al. 1992), which is why the rule also needs the pqq genes.

Required wherever the ring is opened through the diene, because the dearomatising step only means something with the steps that follow. K07538 is specific: every member of that ortholog with a Bakta name keeps it, and Bakta does not hand it to unrelated dehydrogenases.

column2: indole-3-acetamide hydrolase (IaaH), turns indole-3-acetamide into IAA
column11: EcoFoldDB's 'iaaH' entry (UniProt O50173, Pantoea agglomerans, Swiss-Prot, evidence at protein level) is IAA-aspartate hydrolase (gene iaaspH, peptidase M20 family; Chou et al. 1998), which frees IAA from a plant conjugate, so its key is not used. True IaaH belongs to the amidase-signature family. Bakta gives the product name 'Indoleacetamide hydrolase' to many amidase-signature enzymes, so only the iaaH symbol and KO K21801 count, and Baktfold names cannot count. KEGG also uses the symbol iaaH for IAA-aspartate hydrolase (KO K25379), so names containing 'aspart' are vetoed. EC 3.5.1.- is too vague to use.

IaaM and the lysine 2-monooxygenase DavB are homologous flavin enzymes; DavB works in lysine catabolism with the amidase DavA (Revelles et al. 2005). EcoFoldDB has no DavB structure, so DavB proteins best-match its two IaaM structures (UniProt P06617, Pseudomonas savastanoi; Q04564, Gillisella ampelina, formerly Agrobacterium vitis) and a structure hit alone is not enough. Bakta's name 'Tryptophan 2-monooxygenase' also goes to DavB and to unrelated flavin amine oxidases, so only the IaaM KO, EC or symbol count, and Baktfold names cannot count. Any product name containing 'lysine' vetoes the protein.

column2: indole-3-pyruvate decarboxylase (IpdC; includes the phenylpyruvate decarboxylase of Azospirillum)
column11: EcoFoldDB spells this gene idpC. Its two structures are IpdC of Enterobacter cloacae (UniProt P23234; Koga et al. 1991) and the Azospirillum brasilense enzyme (UniProt P51852), which UniProt names indole-3-pyruvate decarboxylase but which is kinetically a phenylpyruvate decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.43) that also makes IAA (Spaepen et al. 2007). EcoFoldDB's background holds pyruvate decarboxylases, benzoylformate decarboxylase, glyoxylate carboligase and acetolactate synthases, so a best hit to idpC counts alone; the layer's borderline flag marks near-ties. Branched-chain keto-acid decarboxylases (Kdc/KdcA type) are not in EcoFoldDB and can be counted as ipdC, which the rule's caveat covers.

EcoFoldDB's ipt (UniProt Q47851) is Etz of the gall-forming Pantoea agglomerans pv. gypsophilae (Lichter et al. 1995). MiaA is in the same family but prenylates tRNA. EcoFoldDB's background holds hundreds of MiaA structures and the plant IPTs, so MiaA proteins normally best-match those and an ipt hit can count alone; any name containing 'tRNA' vetoes the protein, a structure hit included.

Supporting on the enterobactin rule, not in EcoFoldDB. Salmochelin is enterobactin with glucose added, so IroB is what says a strain can make it. The orthologue number is used because the curated orthology defines it as enterobactin C-glucosyltransferase (iroB), so it can find an IroB that the annotation leaves unnamed.

column2: ent-kaurene synthase (class I diterpene synthase of the gibberellin operon)
column11: Bakta names the rhizobial KS after Sinorhizobium fredii NGR234 'Uncharacterized protein y4kS' (UniProt P55537, 301 aa). EcoFoldDB's ks structure is a plant enzyme (UniProt A0A0U4CDK4, Salvia miltiorrhiza, 806 aa) that a bacterial KS cannot cover at the 0.8 coverage filter, so its key is not used. EcoFoldDB lists that entry under KO K04120, but ent-kaurene synthase is K04121.

column8: protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase,? (subunit alpha|alpha (chain|subunit)|small subunit)|alpha subunit of protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase|LigAB,? LigA subunit
column11: Reference: LigA of Sphingobium sp. SYK-6 (P22635, reviewed, evidence at protein level). Both ligA and ligB are needed for protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase activity (Noda et al. 1990). EC 1.13.11.8 is left out because it is shared with the beta chain. Small class III subunit, so a structure hit needs the name to agree. Only names that say alpha, small subunit or LigA count; the bare enzyme name does not, and a single-chain enzyme named 'subunit alpha/beta' counts for both ligA and ligB, because one such chain carries both parts of the enzyme, as PcaA of Pseudarthrobacter phenanthrenivorans does (Tsagogiannis et al. 2021).

column8: protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase,? (subunit (alpha/)?beta|beta (chain|subunit)|large subunit|LigB\b)|(beta subunit|subunit beta) of protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase|class III extradiol (ring-cleavage |)dioxygenase subunit (beta|B)
column11: Reference: LigB of Sphingobium sp. SYK-6 (P22636, reviewed, evidence at protein level). Gallate dioxygenase (GalA) belongs to the same class III family and must be excluded, or every gallate cluster would look like protocatechuate 4,5-cleavage; the price is that a real enzyme named only 'LigB family' is missed. EC 1.13.11.8 is left out because it is shared with the alpha chain. Only names that say beta, large subunit or LigB count; names that say only alpha are vetoed even with the beta-chain KO, and a single-chain enzyme named 'subunit alpha/beta' counts for both ligA and ligB, because one such chain carries both parts of the enzyme, as PcaA of Pseudarthrobacter phenanthrenivorans does (Tsagogiannis et al. 2021).

Reference: LigC of Sphingobium sp. SYK-6 (Q9KWL3, reviewed, evidence at protein level). The catalogue pathway name for this entry covers both protocatechuate and homoprotocatechuate and is copied exactly. Dehydrogenase fold, so structure alone is not enough. Dioxygenase names are vetoed, because a ring-cleavage dioxygenase can carry the LigC KO and EC.

Reference: LigI of Sphingobium sp. SYK-6 (O87170, reviewed, evidence at protein level); in Comamonas the same step (PmdD) is essential for growth on protocatechuate (Kamimura et al. 2010). Amidohydrolase fold, shared with many unrelated hydrolases, so s_alone is false.

Reference: LigJ of Sphingobium sp. SYK-6 (G2IQQ5, reviewed, evidence at protein level). GalB of the gallate pathway does the same step but belongs to a different family of zinc hydratases (Nogales et al. 2011); it is accepted because the step is the same, and the rule still cannot fire in gallate degraders because they lack ligA and ligB. galB's own KO (K16515) is not added because Bakta also puts it on the gallate aldolase GalC. EC 4.2.1.83 is left out because Bakta also puts it on unrelated proteins.

Reference: LigK of Sphingobium sp. SYK-6 (G2IQQ8, reviewed, evidence at protein level); a ligK mutant cannot grow on vanillate or syringate (Hara et al. 2003). LigK and the gallate enzyme GalC share one KEGG orthology (K10218, ligK/galC) and the RraA-like fold, so both are accepted; RraA regulators share that fold, which is why s_alone is false and the RraA wording is vetoed. EC 4.1.3.17 is left out because Bakta also puts it on RraA.

LOG-family proteins carry the cytokinin name in nearly every genome, so log is supporting, not required; as a required gene it would make almost every genome 'partial'. A bacterial LOG does release cytokinins (Samanovic et al. 2015). EcoFoldDB's log structure is a Mycobacterium marinum LOG (UniProt B2HS63), and its background holds other bacterial and plant LOGs.

Structure alone is firmly ruled out: ordinary acyl-CoA and fatty-acid ligases can pass the published thresholds against this entry, adenylation domains being largely interchangeable at this resolution. No enzyme number is listed. The curated salicyl-AMP ligase number, EC 6.2.1.61, names only PchD of pyochelin and PmsE of pseudomonine, while MbtA itself carries the incomplete numbers EC 6.2.1.- and 2.7.7.- and YbtE of yersiniabactin EC 6.3.2.-, so none of them identifies this gene; the mycobactin-specific orthologue number is used instead. The receptor veto matters in a group where uptake proteins routinely carry the siderophore's name. UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the reviewed M. tuberculosis MbtA.

Structure alone is not accepted: large carrier-domain proteins of other systems can pass the published thresholds against this entry. UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the reviewed M. tuberculosis MbtB, the phenyloxazoline synthase that also carries the cluster's aryl carrier domain. 'S-MbtB' is vetoed because the name of MbtA, 'salicyl-AMP ligase/salicyl-S-MbtB synthetase', mentions MbtB.

Supporting only, and the clearest example in the group of why a structure hit is not a trait: the polyketide ketosynthase fold is the fatty-acid synthase fold, so the beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthases of housekeeping fatty-acid synthesis in an ordinary genome can pass the published thresholds against this entry. It must never be a required gene.

Supporting only. EcoFoldDB holds seven mycobactin entries, and this token gives a structure hit to the MbtD entry somewhere to go in the audit table. Like MbtC it is a polyketide synthase of the cluster, so it cannot be required.

This entry can take part in a genuine tie: a large NRPS can score equally well against this entry, the bacillibactin dhbF entry and a third catalogue structure, so which system is reported depends on tie-breaking alone. Such near-ties are what the layer's borderline flag marks, and the reason structure alone is not accepted here. UniProt has the catalogue entry as the M. tuberculosis MbtE peptide synthetase (unreviewed, protein-level evidence). In Mycolicibacterium smegmatis mc2 155, Bakta names MbtE (MSMEG_4511) 'Linear gramicidin synthetase subunit B', the genome's original GenBank annotation, which its UniProt record still carries, and gives no KO; that exact name is accepted, and only as the whole product. The true gramicidin enzyme is named '... synthase subunit B' and does not match, and a call still needs the other mbt genes named and lying together.

Structure alone is not accepted: large carrier-domain proteins of other systems can pass the published thresholds against this entry. UniProt has the catalogue entry as the M. tuberculosis MbtF peptide synthetase (unreviewed, protein-level evidence).

Supporting only, and it could never be anything else: MbtH-like proteins accompany many unrelated NRPS clusters. There is a second, practical reason - the protein is only about 70 residues long, the catalogue's reference protein is 71 residues, and a structure hit of a protein this short can fail the published e-value threshold even at near-full coverage. Short proteins will routinely miss that cut-off, a general point for the layer. The MbtH orthologue number is listed only for completeness.

column2: acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (acylating), last step of the meta pathways
column11: Not in EcoFoldDB, so Bakta-name evidence only. KEGG module M00569 accepts K18366 (bphJ, xylQ, nahO) or K04073 (mhpF) for this step, so both are listed. In the dmp operon this enzyme (DmpF) was shown to be an acylating acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (Shingler et al. 1992). Supporting only, which is why proteins that carry the fermentative symbol adhE with this product name are tolerated; EC 1.2.1.10 is left out because it is shared with fermentative and propanediol-pathway enzymes.

Reference protein UniProt Q52126, reviewed, Pseudomonas putida G7, protein-level evidence. KO K14581 is shared: KEGG uses it both in the naphthalene module and in the salicylate-to-gentisate module (salicylate 5-hydroxylase), and its symbol list includes the nitrobenzene and dinitrotoluene dioxygenase reductases, so this gene only means naphthalene inside its co-localised group. The same reductase is interchangeable with the toluene monooxygenase reductase in experiments, which is a second reason a structure hit cannot name it. EcoFoldDB spells the pathway 'napthalene conversion to salicylaldehyde'; the key copies that spelling exactly and must not be corrected.

Reference protein UniProt P0A185, reviewed, P. putida G7. A known false-name source, kept because it is the only product name this subunit gets; it is harmless because the rule needs eight genes in two co-localised groups. KO K14578 is shared with salicylate 5-hydroxylase and the nitroarene dioxygenases, so it also needs the co-localised partners. The look-ahead stops the pattern from matching the reductase subunit.

Reference protein UniProt P0A110, reviewed, P. putida G7, protein-level evidence. The substrate-determining subunit. Ring-hydroxylating alpha subunits are near-identical in structure across substrates, so this gene never counts from a structure hit alone; KO K14579 carries the nitrobenzene and dinitrotoluene dioxygenase symbols as well, so the name, not the KO, is what distinguishes naphthalene. A name given to both subunits at once ('large and small subunits') counts for neither.

Reference protein UniProt P0A112, reviewed, P. putida G7. Alternative nag and ndo symbols cover the Ralstonia and other naming schemes. KO K14580 is shared: its symbol list also holds the nitrobenzene and dinitrotoluene dioxygenase beta subunits (nbzAd, dntAd), so like the other three components this gene only means naphthalene inside its co-localised group. A name given to both subunits at once ('large and small subunits') counts for neither.

Reference protein UniProt P0A169, reviewed, P. putida G7, but annotated by homology rather than experiment. A short-chain dehydrogenase, and the same enzyme also works on dibenzothiophene dihydrodiol (the catalogue lists that second EC); only the naphthalene EC is used here so the gene is not claimed from a different substrate. 'D-xylose' is vetoed because some annotations give this activity to a sugar dehydrogenase.

Reference protein UniProt P11861, reviewed, P. putida G7, protein-level evidence. An extradiol dioxygenase of the same class as the catechol 2,3-dioxygenase and the biphenyl enzyme, so sequence agreement is required.

Reference protein UniProt Q51948, reviewed, P. putida G7, protein-level evidence. Bakta also hands this product name to glutathione-S-transferase-like proteins, sometimes with an unrelated symbol. The isomerisation it catalyses also happens slowly without an enzyme, so a naphthalene degrader with an unnamed isomerase is a possible false negative; the gene is kept required because it is in the operon of every characterised nah and nag degrader and in the KEGG module.

Reference protein UniProt Q51947, reviewed, P. putida G7, protein-level evidence. The second alternative is anchored to the bare product name 'Hydratase-aldolase', which is exactly how the catalogue names the phenanthrene enzyme phdG, so that wording is shared with the phenanthrene pathway; it is accepted only because the gene sits inside a four-gene co-localised group, and an EcoFoldDB hit on the phenanthrene entry is a different key and never counts here.

Reference protein UniProt P0A391, reviewed, P. putida G7, but annotated by homology and with the weakest annotation score of the set. A textbook case for s_alone false: the aldehyde dehydrogenase fold gives very strong structure scores across completely different substrates, so a hit here is not evidence of this gene. Supporting only, because the trait stops at salicylaldehyde and the catalogue holds this gene under a separate pathway.

column8: nitrate reductase catalytic subunit NapA|periplasmic nitrate reductase,? (alpha|catalytic|large)|nitrate reductase \(cytochrome\)
column11: Periplasmic nitrate reductase (Nap), catalytic subunit. A structure hit alone does not count: the assimilatory nitrate reductase (NasA) shares the molybdenum (bis-MGD) catalytic fold and can best-hit the NapA structure (Richardson et al. 2001 describe the three related classes). The symbol napA also names unrelated proteins (a Na+/H+ antiporter, a class B acid phosphatase), so the symbol counts only with a nitrate-reductase name or KO K02567.

column2: periplasmic nitrate reductase, small diheme cytochrome c subunit
column8: periplasmic nitrate reductase,? electron transfer subunit|nitrate reductase cytochrome c-type subunit|nitrate reductase electron transfer subunit|\bNapB\b
column11: Small diheme cytochrome c partner of NapA. EcoFoldDB lists napB with K02567, the NapA KO; the NapB KO is K02568, used here. The EcoFoldDB structure is E. coli NapB, which helps where Bakta misnames NapB (in E. coli K-12 it is called NapH).

column2: respiratory nitrate reductase, alpha subunit (NarG; NarZ in the second E. coli enzyme)
column8: nitrate reductase (Z )?subunit alpha|respiratory nitrate reductase( \d)? alpha|nitrate reductase alpha (chain|subunit)
column11: Membrane-bound respiratory nitrate reductase (Nar), catalytic subunit; NarZ of the second E. coli enzyme also counts. KEGG K00370 is shared with the nitrite oxidoreductase NxrA of nitrite oxidisers (EcoFoldDB files nxrA separately), and Bakta sometimes puts K00370 on NarH, which the exclusion handles. Assimilatory nitrate reductases (NasA, NasC, NarB) feed nitrogen into biomass and are excluded. Bakta's plain 'Nitrate reductase' is not used: it also sits on unrelated proteins (for example the bacterioferritin-associated ferredoxin Bfd).

column2: respiratory nitrate reductase, beta subunit (NarH; NarY)
column8: nitrate reductase (Z )?subunit beta|respiratory nitrate reductase( \d)? beta|nitrate reductase beta (chain|subunit)
column11: Iron-sulphur electron-transfer subunit of Nar (NarY in the second E. coli enzyme). KEGG K00371 is shared with NxrB.

column2: respiratory nitrate reductase, gamma subunit (membrane cytochrome b; NarI; NarV)
column8: nitrate reductase (subunit )?gamma|respiratory nitrate reductase( \d)? gamma|nitrate reductase \(gamma subunit\)
column11: Membrane cytochrome b that anchors Nar (NarV in the second E. coli enzyme).

column2: FeMo-cofactor biosynthesis protein NifB (radical SAM enzyme that makes the cofactor core)
column11: Not in EcoFoldDB; names only. Bakta also gives the symbol nifB to other radical-SAM 'Fe-S oxidoreductases' in non-fixers, so the symbol counts only together with a NifB name or the NifB KO (K02585). Only names that say NifB are accepted, because generic 'cofactor biosynthesis protein' names also fit NifX/NafY-type proteins. Protochlorophyllide reductase names are vetoed, because such proteins can carry the NifB KO.

column8: nitrogenase molybdenum-iron protein,? (alpha|subunit alpha)|nitrogenase MoFe protein alpha|dinitrogenase alpha
column11: Excludes the vanadium and iron-only alpha chains (VnfD, AnfD; KEGG files AnfD under the same KO) and the paralogue NifE. In Anabaena-type heterocyst-forming cyanobacteria an 11-kb element inside nifD is cut out only in heterocysts (Golden et al. 1985), so in an assembled genome nifD is shortened and about a dozen genes sit between it and nifK (12 in Nostoc sp. PCC 7120); this is one reason the rule does not require nif genes to sit together. Bakta also writes the symbol nifD on NifH, NifK, NifE and NifN proteins and on the protochlorophyllide reductase subunit BchB, so the names of those proteins (NifH, frxC, NifN, reductase) are vetoed, as is the recombinase of the nifD excision element.

column2: FeMo-cofactor biosynthesis protein NifE (assembly scaffold, related to NifD)
column11: Not in EcoFoldDB, so only Bakta or Baktfold names find it. NifE is related to NifD; with NifN it forms the scaffold on which the FeMo-cofactor is built, and NifE, NifN and NifB are what separate real nitrogen fixers from genomes with nitrogenase-like genes (Dos Santos et al. 2012). Vanadium-cofactor (VnfE) names are excluded.

column2: nitrogenase iron protein (Fe protein, dinitrogenase reductase)
column11: Bakta often gives no gene symbol, only the name 'Nitrogenase iron protein', so the name pattern does the work. A structure hit alone does not count: the Fe protein shares its P-loop ATPase fold with non-nitrogenase proteins such as the flagellar regulator FleN/FlhG and MinD/ParA, and with the chlorophyll-synthesis enzymes BchL/BchX. The pattern also accepts the Fe proteins of the alternative nitrogenases (same name); harmless, because every genome known to carry an alternative nitrogenase also carries the molybdenum one. Names of the DraT/DraG enzymes that switch the Fe protein off are excluded. The catalogue's AnfH entry, the iron-only nitrogenase Fe protein of Azotobacter vinelandii, is mapped to this gene as well, so a structure hit on it is not lost; because a structure hit never counts on its own here, it can only confirm a 'nitrogenase iron protein' name. Names of nitrogenase component 1 (the molybdenum-iron protein) are vetoed, because such proteins can carry the NifH KO, and so are 'nitrogenase reductase-associated' proteins.

column8: nitrogenase molybdenum-iron protein,? (beta|subunit beta)|nitrogenase MoFe protein beta|dinitrogenase beta
column11: Excludes the vanadium and iron-only beta chains and the paralogue NifN. nifK normally follows nifD in the same operon (nifHDK, or nifDK where nifH is separate), but the rule does not require co-localisation (see nifD).

column2: FeMo-cofactor biosynthesis protein NifN (assembly scaffold, related to NifK)
column11: Not in EcoFoldDB; names only. Related to NifK; partner of NifE in FeMo-cofactor assembly. VnfN names are excluded.

column8: copper-containing nitrite reductase|Cu-containing nitrite reductase|nitrite reductase,? copper-containing|copper nitrite reductase|\bAniA\b|\bNirK\b
column11: Copper nitrite reductase (AniA in Neisseria). A structure hit alone does not count: two-domain multicopper oxidases (small laccases) share the NirK fold. Bakta's plain 'Nitrite reductase' is not used, because it also sits on assimilatory and unrelated proteins.

Cytochrome cd1 nitrite reductase. A structure hit alone does not count: NirN, a NirS relative encoded in the same nir gene cluster, and other cytochromes c can give strong hits. Bakta usually names NirS just 'nitrite reductase' with the symbol nirS, so the symbol carries the sequence evidence; the plain name without the symbol is not used. '-like' names are vetoed.

Nitrilases belong to the large carbon-nitrogen hydrolase superfamily (with amidases, N-carbamoylputrescine amidase and others), and structure cannot tell their substrate, so s_alone is false. EcoFoldDB's three nitrilase structures are a Paraburkholderia phymatum nitrilase (UniProt B2JQY2), the bromoxynil-specific nitrilase of Klebsiella (P10045, gene bxn) and a metagenomic nitrilase (Q6RWK4); none is the indole-3-acetonitrile nitrilase of Alcaligenes faecalis (Kobayashi et al. 1993), so the catalogue itself is not specific for indole-3-acetonitrile. The symbol nit1 is not listed because Bakta also gives it to nitrilase-like proteins of other families. Aliphatic nitrilases are vetoed because their preferred substrates are aliphatic nitriles.

NodA is the N-acyltransferase that attaches the fatty acid to the Nod factor backbone; its protein family (Pfam PF02474) is specific to nodulation genes. A structure hit alone is still not counted, to keep the three nod genes on the same footing. A name that describes a stretch of nodulation genes rather than one protein is vetoed.

column9: NodB-like|NodB homology|y domain|nodulation genes|nodulation protein A\b
column11: NodB is a chitooligosaccharide deacetylase (John et al. 1993) whose domain is the polysaccharide deacetylase ('NodB homology') domain shared with the PgaB/IcaB deacetylases of biofilm polysaccharide clusters. Those clusters also contain GT2 synthases that resemble NodC, so a structure hit alone is not counted for nodB or nodC. A name that describes a stretch of nodulation genes rather than one protein is vetoed, and a protein named 'nodulation protein A' never counts here.

column8: nodulation protein C\b|\bNodC\b|chitooligosaccharide synthase|chitin oligosaccharide synthase
column11: NodC is a GT2 glycosyltransferase related to chitin and cellulose synthases (Atkinson & Long 1992), and other GT2 proteins can best-match its structure. A name that describes a stretch of nodulation genes rather than one protein is vetoed.

column2: NodI, ATP-binding subunit of the Nod factor exporter
column11: Supporting only. No KO is used, because the ABC-transporter KOs are generic.

column2: NodJ, permease of the Nod factor exporter
column11: Supporting only. KO K09694 is not used, because Bakta also assigns it to generic ABC permeases.

column2: nitric oxide reductase, cytochrome b subunit of the cytochrome c-dependent enzyme (cNOR)
column11: Large subunit of the cytochrome c-dependent NO reductase (cNOR). The symbol norB also names a Staphylococcus efflux pump, so the symbol counts only with an NO-reductase name or KO K04561. Excluded: flavorubredoxin NorV (NO detoxification), regulators, the NorD/NorQ/NorE/NorF assembly proteins, NorC names, and the three forms that mark the single-chain quinol enzyme - 'large subunit', 'quinol' and 'qNor' - so a protein named, for example, 'Nitric oxide reductase qNor type' gives a norZ line only. EC 1.7.2.5 is left out because it is also written on NorC and NorE entries.

column2: nitric oxide reductase, cytochrome c subunit of cNOR
column11: Small membrane cytochrome c of cNOR. Bakta often gives it only a generic cytochrome c name, so a structure hit counts on its own; the rule's co-localisation with norB stops a stray cytochrome c elsewhere from completing the trait. The symbol counts only with an NO-reductase name (norC also names a Staphylococcus efflux pump). NorB names are vetoed, because they can carry 'cytochrome c', as in the enzyme name 'nitric-oxide reductase (cytochrome c)' and in qNOR names with a 'cytochrome c-like domain'; so are the bare enzyme name and the NorE name 'cytochrome c oxidase subunit'.

column2: quinol-dependent nitric oxide reductase (qNOR; one chain, no NorC partner)
column11: Quinol-dependent NO reductase (qNOR): one long chain (about 750 amino acids) with no NorC partner, also used by non-denitrifiers to detoxify NO (Hendriks et al. 2000). RefSeq calls it 'nitric-oxide reductase large subunit'; UniProt-style names call it 'nitric oxide reductase subunit B', and when Bakta uses that name the protein counts as norB instead, so the trait shows as partial (norC missing). EcoFoldDB's NorB structure is the short cNOR subunit, which a qNOR does not cover, so there is no structure route. A product name that says 'qNor' is vetoed on norB, so such a protein reaches this token alone.

column2: periplasmic copper-binding protein NosD (needed to build the CuZ centre of NosZ)
column11: Supporting. Bakta gives the symbol nosD to unrelated proteins that only share NosD's beta-helix domain ('NosD domain-containing protein'); those names are excluded and the symbol needs a NosD name or the NosD KO.

column2: NosF, ATP-binding subunit of the NosDFY copper-processing system
column11: Supporting; ATP-binding subunit of the NosDFY system that loads copper into NosZ.
Supporting; copper chaperone for NosZ.

column2: NosY, membrane subunit of the NosDFY copper-processing system
