column11: Supporting; membrane subunit of NosDFY. Bakta often names it only 'ABC transporter permease' but keeps the specific KO K19341.

column2: nitrous oxide reductase (both the Tat-exported clade I and the Sec-exported clade II forms)
column11: N2O reductase; the name pattern covers both the Tat-exported (clade I, 'TAT-dependent') and Sec-exported (clade II) enzymes. Excluded: the 'nitrous oxide-stimulated promoter' family (YgbA-like proteins common in enterobacteria) and the Nos accessory and regulatory proteins.

Bakta names these decarboxylases 'carboxynorspermidine decarboxylase'; some carry the KO and EC of carboxyaminopropylagmatine decarboxylase (CAPADC; K27684, EC 4.1.1.127), the agmatine-route paralogue that also leads to spermidine (Xi et al. 2023), and both count. A protein with that KO may be named 'Lysine/ornithine decarboxylase'; it is counted here, not as ornithine decarboxylase. EcoFoldDB's nspC structure (UniProt Q5QCP2, Herminiimonas arsenicoxydans) is a fold-type III decarboxylase; the diaminopimelate decarboxylases of the background compete with it.
The ring-opening step. Crotonase fold, so sequence or Baktfold agreement is required; K07539 is specific and is kept for all annotated members.

KO K16055 and one of EcoFoldDB's two otsA structures are bifunctional synthase-phosphatases; that structure is an archaeal enzyme of about 730 residues, so an ordinary bacterial OtsA of about 460 residues cannot cover enough of it to pass the coverage filter. A genuinely bifunctional protein counts for otsA by structure and for otsB by name or KO.

OtsB is a HAD-superfamily phosphatase, a very large family, so a structure hit alone is not counted; one of its two catalogue structures is also only an archaeal 'trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase-related protein', a second reason not to trust structure alone here. otsA and otsB are not always adjacent (in Mycobacterium tuberculosis otsA and otsB2 lie about 120 kb apart), so they need not sit together.

column8: phenylacetyl-CoA (1,2-)?epoxidase.{0,25}(PaaA|subunit A|alpha subunit|subunit alpha|catalytic subunit)\b|ring-oxydation complex protein 1\b|phenylacetate-CoA oxygenase.{0,20}Paa[AG]\b
column11: The key copies the catalogue's misspelt pathway name 'phenylacteate degradation'. The reference (UniProt Q845J6, Pseudomonas sp. Y2, TrEMBL, not curated) is in the PaaA family (InterPro IPR011881) although UniProt gives its gene as paaG: in the older Pseudomonas putida letters the epoxidase subunits are PaaG to PaaK, which is why both letter sets are in the pattern. The symbol counts only with a matching product or KO because UniProt also uses paaA for ATPases and ligases. EC 1.14.13.149 is left out because it is also given to paaC. s_alone is false: the family is specific to this pathway, but PaaA shares the di-iron four-helix-bundle (ferritin-like) fold with other oxygenases and the catalogue holds a single reference, so a structure hit needs a sequence name; Bakta names this subunit consistently, so little is lost. Names that say PaaC or PaaI are vetoed, because such PaaC-type proteins can carry the PaaA KO.

column8: phenylacetyl-CoA (1,2-)?epoxidase.{0,25}(PaaB|subunit B|regulatory subunit)\b|ring-oxydation complex protein 2\b|phenylacetate-CoA oxygenase.{0,20}Paa[BH]\b
column11: The reference (Q845J5, Pseudomonas sp. Y2, TrEMBL, not curated, gene paaH in the older letters) is in the PaaB family (IPR009359). A small protein of about 95 residues, so structure matches carry little weight and s_alone is false. The symbol needs a matching product because UniProt also uses paaB for the ring isomerase PaaG.

column8: phenylacetyl-CoA (1,2-)?epoxidase.{0,25}(PaaC|subunit C|beta subunit|subunit beta|structural subunit)\b|ring-oxydation complex protein 3\b|phenylacetate-CoA oxygenase.{0,20}Paa[CI]\b|^PaaI$
column11: The reference (Q845J4, Pseudomonas sp. Y2, TrEMBL, not curated, gene paaI in the older letters) is in the PaaC family (IPR011882). The symbol needs a matching product because UniProt also uses paaC for a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase. s_alone is false for the same reason as paaA.

column2: PaaD, accessory protein of the 1,2-phenylacetyl-CoA epoxidase (not needed for catalysis)
column8: phenylacetyl-CoA (1,2-)?epoxidase.{0,25}(PaaD|subunit D)\b|phenylacet(ate|ic acid) degradation protein PaaD|phenylacetate-CoA oxygenase.{0,20}Paa[DJ]\b|subunit of phenylacetate degradation enzyme
column11: Not in EcoFoldDB. Supporting only: PaaD is not needed for epoxidase activity in vitro (Grishin et al. 2011) and probably helps the complex mature. KEGG module M00878 lists it, so this is one place where the rule is deliberately less strict than KEGG.

column8: phenylacetyl-CoA (1,2-)?epoxidase.{0,25}(PaaE|subunit E|reductase subunit)\b|ring-oxydation complex protein 5\b|phenylacetate-CoA oxygenase/reductase|phenylacetate-CoA oxygenase.{0,20}Paa[EK]\b
column11: The reference (Q845J2, Pseudomonas sp. Y2, TrEMBL, not curated, gene paaK in the older letters) is in the PaaE family (IPR011884). A ferredoxin-NADP reductase-type flavoprotein with a ferredoxin domain, a large family, so s_alone is false. The paaK entry vetoes every oxygenase name, so one protein never counts as both genes.

KO K01692 is left out because it is the generic enoyl-CoA hydratase group. The reference (Q845K2, Pseudomonas sp. Y2, TrEMBL, not curated, gene paaA in the older letters) is a plain crotonase-fold enzyme. Supporting only, which absorbs the matches outside paa clusters.

The reference (Q845K1, Pseudomonas sp. Y2, TrEMBL, not curated, gene paaB in the older letters) is in the same InterPro family as E. coli PaaG (IPR011968). Crotonase fold. Supporting only; oxygenase names are vetoed because the older letter PaaG means the epoxidase alpha subunit.
The reference (P76083) is the Swiss-Prot E. coli PaaH. KO K00074 is left out because it is the generic 3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase group. Supporting only.

The reference (Q845J8, Pseudomonas sp. Y2, TrEMBL, not curated) is a thiolase of the beta-ketoadipyl-CoA thiolase family (IPR012793), which also holds PcaF; the two cannot be told apart by name, so paaJ is never required.

The reference (Q9L9C1) is the Swiss-Prot phenylacetate-CoA ligase of Aromatoleum evansii, with protein-level evidence. AMP-forming (ANL) ligase superfamily; the PaaK family itself also holds ligases of other pathways, so s_alone is false and Bakta's 'family protein' names, given to family-level matches, are vetoed. Not in the co-localised group, because in some actinobacteria the ligase sits far from the epoxidase subunits.

column2: PaaN-type aldehyde dehydrogenase found in paa clusters that lack PaaZ
column8: phenylacetic acid degradation protein PaaN|phenylacetate degradation protein PaaN|^PaaN$
column11: Teufel et al. 2011 showed that many paa clusters carry an NAD-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase in place of PaaZ, with the ring-opening hydratase encoded elsewhere; the example in that paper is PacL of Aromatoleum aromaticum. The symbol PaaN itself comes from the aldehyde dehydrogenase family InterPro calls PaaN (IPR011966), which also holds the dehydrogenases of the benzoyl-CoA oxygenase (box) pathway, so the name alone is weak evidence. KEGG has no orthology group for it. Supporting only.

column2: PaaZ, bifunctional oxepin-CoA hydrolase / 3-oxo-5,6-dehydrosuberyl-CoA semialdehyde dehydrogenase
column11: The reference (P77455) is the Swiss-Prot Escherichia coli PaaZ. Supporting only: many degraders carry an NAD-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase in the cluster instead and encode the ring-opening hydratase elsewhere (Teufel et al. 2011), so a paa cluster without PaaZ can still be a working pathway.

column2: phosphate-insensitive alkaline phosphatase PafA (also Sphingomonas PhoK; same family)
column11: Phosphate-insensitive alkaline phosphatase PafA, common in Bacteroidetes and made even when phosphate is plentiful (Lidbury et al. 2022); Sphingomonas PhoK is the same family, so EcoFoldDB's phoK structure counts here. A structure hit alone does not count (the alkaline-phosphatase superfamily is large). The symbol pafA also names the Pup-protein ligase of Actinobacteria, which is excluded.

Reference: PcaB of A. baylyi ADP1 (Q59092, reviewed, evidence at protein level). Same fold as adenylosuccinate lyase, argininosuccinate lyase, aspartase and fumarase, which every genome has and which are close in structure to this reference; only better hits to non-catalogue structures keep them out, so a structure hit needs the name to agree. Bakta hands the purB symbol to the real pcaB in enterobacteria, which is why only the product counts.

Reference: PcaC of A. baylyi ADP1 (P20370, reviewed, function inferred from homology). The carboxymuconolactone decarboxylase family is large (AhpD-like proteins included) and its members can score just short of the cut-off against this small structure with no better hit to stop them, so a structure hit never counts alone, even though that would rescue the misnamed P. aeruginosa enzyme. The actinobacterial fusion PcaL (KEGG K14727) counts as both pcaC and pcaD.

column2: 3-oxoadipate enol-lactonase (beta-ketoadipate enol-lactone hydrolase), shared by the catechol and protocatechuate branches
column11: Reference: PP_1380 of P. putida KT2440 (Q88N36), the pcaD of its pcaBDC operon; an unreviewed UniProt entry whose function is inferred from homology. The alpha/beta hydrolase fold is shared by a great many unrelated enzymes, so s_alone is false and generic fold names are vetoed outright. The cost is real: where Bakta names the true enzyme only 'alpha/beta fold hydrolase', as in some actinobacterial pca clusters, the gene is lost. The actinobacterial fusion PcaL (KEGG K14727) carries both the decarboxylase and the lactonase names and counts as both pcaC and pcaD.

Not in EcoFoldDB, so Bakta-name evidence only; supporting in both beta-ketoadipate rules. KEGG K07823 is pcaF's own orthology and is listed; K02615 stays out because it is the phenylacetate-pathway paaJ, which also accepts 3-oxoadipyl-CoA, so pcaF and paaJ are hard to separate by name and neither is ever required.

Reference: PcaG of Pseudomonas putida (P00436, reviewed, evidence at protein level). s_alone is true because this is the chain that goes missing from Bakta's names, and it is safe because the catalogue holds the competing intradiol references (the beta chain, catA, hydroxyquinol 1,2-dioxygenase), so the best hit chooses between named enzymes. No EC is listed because Bakta gives 1.13.11.3 to both chains. The enzyme is built from alpha and beta chains together (Bull & Ballou 1981), which is why both are required and must sit together. Cycloisomerase names are vetoed, because a 3-carboxy-cis,cis-muconate cycloisomerase can carry the PcaG KO. Beta-chain names are not vetoed: Bakta can give this chain the beta chain's name and KO, and a veto would also cancel the structure hit that s_alone relies on.

Reference: PcaH of A. baylyi ADP1 (P20372, reviewed, evidence at protein level). s_alone is kept true for symmetry with the alpha chain, so that a genome where Bakta mislabels the pair the other way round is not lost, and it is safe for the same reason (the competing intradiol enzymes are in the catalogue). Because a pcaH name can sit on the wrong chain, the rule still needs the pair found together. Alpha-chain names are not vetoed: Bakta can give this chain the alpha chain's name, and a veto would also cancel the structure hit that s_alone relies on.

Supporting only, because salicylate is the starter unit of yersiniabactin and mycobactin as well as pyochelin. The orthologue number used here is the salicylate-pathway one, not the menaquinone or enterobactin one.

Supporting only. The exclusion is the interesting part: in yersiniabactin and mycobactin producers the two salicylate steps are fused into one salicylate synthase with its own orthologue number, which shares this enzyme number, so vetoing that name stops a yersiniabactin cluster contributing a pyochelin gene line.

Supporting only. It is included because it is the one other pyochelin gene the annotation marks reliably by orthologue number, which makes the audit table informative in genomes where the four synthetase names are missing. A type II editing thioesterase is a proofreading accessory and clusters without it still make the siderophore, so it must not be required.

Not in EcoFoldDB. The equivalent step in yersiniabactin and mycobactin is YbtE and MbtA, which the annotation names explicitly, so requiring the pyochelin name keeps the three systems apart. The enzyme number for salicyl-AMP ligase is shared with PmsE of pseudomonine, so the pseudomonine names are vetoed here and the pyochelin names on the pmsE entry: one protein must not be counted under two systems.

Not in EcoFoldDB. PchE and PchF are consecutive synthetase modules and are required together, which distinguishes pyochelin from the other salicylate-capped siderophores that use the same starter unit. The orthologue number is pyochelin-specific in the curated orthology and counts where the annotation attaches it; otherwise the product name does the work.

Structure alone is not accepted: large carrier-domain proteins of other systems can pass the published thresholds against this entry. The pattern names the protein, not the siderophore: matching the siderophore's name rather than the protein's name makes every gene in a cluster indistinguishable, so one named protein would satisfy a whole required set.

A direct symbol collision: the pchG symbol is also used for the yersiniabactin reductase YbtU, so the symbol counts only when the product names pyochelin, and the YbtU orthologue number is not listed. A match by orthologue number alone is accepted: the PchG orthologue number can find a genuine PchG that the annotation names only generically, inside a complete pyochelin cluster. Structure alone is not accepted either: other Gfo/Idh/MocA-family oxidoreductases can pass the thresholds against this entry, and UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is itself a Gfo/Idh/MocA-family protein.

column2: single-component phenol hydroxylase (flavoprotein monooxygenase, TbuD/PheA type)
column11: The token is spelt pheA_phenol so that the rules table cannot be read as carrying the phenylalanine-biosynthesis gene, which is what the symbol pheA means on most proteins that carry it; the EcoFoldDB key keeps the catalogue's own name. The catalogue's reference protein is UniProt P15245, the phenol hydroxylase of the yeast Cutaneotrichosporon cutaneum, and its EC 1.14.13.7 is the NADPH-dependent fungal reaction in ExPASy, so a structure hit never counts on its own here. The bacterial single-component enzymes this token is meant for are TbuD of Ralstonia pickettii (UniProt Q01551, reviewed) and PheA of Pseudomonas sp. EST1001 (P31020, reviewed), both flavoproteins that hydroxylate phenol and the cresols. KO K03380 and EC 1.14.13.7 are deliberately not used, because Bakta also puts them on generic FAD-binding monooxygenases and on 3-hydroxybenzoate hydroxylase, and a loose route would report the enzyme on proteins that are not phenol hydroxylases. Supporting only: a name match is reported beside the multicomponent hydroxylase and never calls the trait. The symbol mphA is not accepted either, since it is the macrolide phosphotransferase; the Acinetobacter phenol hydroxylase genes mphK to mphP sit in the dmp entries.

column2: C-P lyase core complex subunit PhnG
column11: Subunit of the core C-P lyase complex (PhnG, H, I, J and K form one complex; Jochimsen et al. 2011). Names of PhnJ and PhnK proteins are vetoed, because such proteins can carry the PhnG KO or symbol. The veto reads 'protein PhnK', so a structure title of the whole C-P lyase complex that mentions PhnK does not cancel a PhnG structure hit.

column2: C-P lyase core complex subunit PhnH
column11: Subunit of the core C-P lyase complex. Names of PhnJ are vetoed, because such proteins can carry the symbol phnH.

column2: C-P lyase core complex subunit PhnI (makes ribose-1-phosphonate-5-triphosphate)
column11: Subunit of the core complex; with PhnG, PhnH and PhnL it makes ribose-1-phosphonate-5-triphosphate from ATP and the phosphonate (Kamat et al. 2011). Names of PhnG, PhnH and PhnJ are vetoed, because such proteins can carry the PhnI KO.

column2: C-P lyase subunit PhnJ (the radical enzyme that cuts the C-P bond)
column11: Subunit of the core complex; the radical enzyme that breaks the C-P bond (Kamat et al. 2011). Bakta often names it only 'Alpha-D-ribose 1-methylphosphonate 5-phosphate C-P lyase', without a symbol. PhnK protein names are vetoed, because such proteins can carry the PhnJ KO and EC. The veto reads 'protein PhnK', so a structure title of the whole C-P lyase complex that mentions PhnK does not cancel a PhnJ structure hit.

column2: C-P lyase core complex subunit PhnK (ABC-ATPase-like)
column11: Core-complex subunit with an ABC-ATPase-like fold; not in EcoFoldDB, so names only. Bakta gives the symbol phnK to many ordinary ABC-transporter ATPases in genomes without any phn genes, so the symbol counts only with a PhnK name; 'phosphonate-specific ATP-binding protein' is accepted as one. Structure titles of the whole C-P lyase complex ('E. coli C-P lyase bound to a PhnK ABC dimer ...') are vetoed: Baktfold gives such a title to a protein that matches any subunit of the complex, so it does not say the protein is PhnK.

ABC-ATPase-like subunit that works with PhnG, PhnH and PhnI (Kamat et al. 2011); not part of the core complex, so not in the co-localised group. PhnL written as part of 'PhnK/PhnL' does not count: that is how structure titles of the whole C-P lyase complex name it, and Baktfold gives such a title to a protein that matches any subunit. This is done in the pattern rather than by a veto, so a structure hit still counts.

column2: C-P lyase pathway hydrolase PhnM (ribose-1-phosphonate-5-triphosphate diphosphatase)
column11: Hydrolyses ribose-1-phosphonate-5-triphosphate (Kamat et al. 2011). It can sit away from the phnGHIJKL cluster, next to phnN, so it is required but not co-localised.

column2: ribose 1,5-bisphosphokinase PhnN (last step of the C-P lyase pathway, to PRPP)
column11: Supporting: ribose 1,5-bisphosphokinase, the last step to PRPP; not strictly needed for C-P lyase activity (Metcalf & Wanner 1993).

Supporting: phosphodiesterase that opens the cyclic phosphate made by PhnJ; not strictly needed (Metcalf & Wanner 1993). Bakta gives the symbol phnP to many metallo-beta-lactamase-fold hydrolases, so the symbol needs a PhnP name or KO K06167; that KO also lands on a few such hydrolases in genomes without C-P lyase.

column2: alkaline phosphatase, PhoA family (E. coli PhoA type)
column11: PhoA-family alkaline phosphatase (E. coli PhoA; in Bacillus both PhoA and PhoB are of this type). A structure hit alone does not count: EcoFoldDB's phoA entries mix a real PhoA with two Pseudomonas aeruginosa 'alkaline phosphatase L' (DING) proteins shaped like phosphate-binding proteins (PstS) and with a metallophosphoesterase. Bakta's plain 'Alkaline phosphatase' counts only with the phoA symbol or KO K01077, because the same name also sits on DedA-family membrane proteins (KO K03975). UniProt lists phoA among the gene names of the DING protein LapA, so phosphate-binding-protein, PstS and disulfide-reductase names are vetoed.

column2: alkaline phosphatase D (PhoD family, secreted phosphomonoesterase/diesterase)
column8: alkaline phosphatase D\b|alkaline phosphatase PhoD|PhoD-like phosphatase|PhoD family
column11: PhoD-family alkaline phosphatase (phosphomonoesterase and diesterase), found in 20 bacterial phyla and most abundant in soil (Ragot et al. 2015). The single EcoFoldDB structure is Bacillus subtilis PhoD, so a structure hit counts on its own.

column2: class A non-specific acid phosphatase (PhoN, PhoC)
column8: acid phosphatase Pho[NC]\b|class A (non-?specific )?acid phosphatase|non-?specific acid phosphatase
column11: Class A non-specific acid phosphatase (PhoN, PhoC; PAP2 family). EcoFoldDB files its class A structure (Providencia stuartii PhoN) under the aphA key, so that key is listed for both aphA and phoN; with s_alone=false on both, Bakta's name decides which gene a structure hit supports. The symbols phoN and phoC need a phosphatase name or KO K09474, because phoC is also used for other genes.

column2: alkaline phosphatase PhoX (calcium-dependent, beta-propeller; Pfam PF05787, formerly DUF839)
column11: Calcium-dependent, Tat-exported alkaline phosphatase with a beta-propeller fold (Pfam PF05787, formerly DUF839), widespread in bacteria (Sebastian & Ammerman 2009). Not in EcoFoldDB. Bakta gives the symbol phoX to a dTDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase in some genomes, which the exclusion removes; other phoX-symbol proteins with vague names ('Phosphatase', 'Cell surface protein') are kept. RefSeq also uses the gene symbol phoX for a PstS-like 'phosphate ABC transporter substrate-binding protein PhoX'; transporter and binding-protein names are vetoed.

column2: phthalate 4,5-dioxygenase, reductase component (PDR/VanB family flavo-iron-sulfur protein)
column3: pht2@phthalate conversion to protocatechuic acid route 1
column11: The catalogue reference (A0A5P9CJ71, Vibrio aquimaris, TrEMBL, not curated) is a 92-residue ferredoxin domain, not a full reductase (about 320 residues, as in the Swiss-Prot P. putida Pht2, Q05182). Under EcoFoldDB's coverage filters a real reductase cannot pass against it, so a structure hit can only come from small ferredoxins and never counts alone. PDR/VanB family: vanillate-demethylase reductases look alike and sometimes carry phthalate names.

column2: phthalate 4,5-dioxygenase, oxygenase component (a single type of subunit, no beta subunit)
column3: pht3@phthalate conversion to protocatechuic acid route 1
column8: \bphthalate 4,5-dioxygenase.{0,30}(oxygenase subunit|oxygenase component|large subunit|alpha subunit)|^phthalate dioxygenase( oxygenase)?( subunit| component)?$
column11: The reference (Q05183) is the Swiss-Prot P. putida phthalate 4,5-dioxygenase oxygenase. It works with a reductase only and has no beta subunit (Batie et al. 1987). A Rieske oxygenase of the vanillate-demethylase type, so s_alone is false. EC 1.14.12.7 is left out because it is also given to the reductase. The tokens pht2 to pht5 keep the P. putida gene names the catalogue uses; Burkholderia calls the same genes ophA1, ophA2, ophB and ophC. The bare enzyme name 'phthalate 4,5-dioxygenase' does not count: it is also the name of the reductase and of unrelated flavin reductases.

column3: pht4@phthalate conversion to protocatechuic acid route 1
column11: The catalogue reference (A0A6N8HLC2, an automatically named protein from a Lentibacillus genome) has been deleted from UniProt. It is a Gfo/Idh/MocA-family oxidoreductase, the same family as the Swiss-Prot P. putida Pht4 (Q05184) and Burkholderia OphB, but that family is large, so s_alone is false. '4,5-dihydroxyphthalate dehydrogenase' is the usual database name, although the enzyme acts on the dihydrodiol.

column3: pht5@phthalate conversion to protocatechuic acid route 1
column11: The reference (Q05185) is the Swiss-Prot P. putida enzyme (258 residues); the Burkholderia and Comamonas decarboxylases have about 330. These enzymes have the fold of periplasmic substrate-binding proteins (Pfam SsuA/THI5-like or phosphonate-binding domains; the SsuA/THI5-like domain alone covers about 50,000 proteins in InterPro), so transporter binding proteins look alike and s_alone is false. The same name is given automatically to some unrelated proteins in fungi and actinobacteria; the co-localised set guards against them.

column8: \bphthalate 3,4-dioxygenase.{0,30}(alpha|large)|\bphthalate dioxygenase.{0,15}(alpha|large) subunit|large subunit of phthalate dioxygenase|^PhtAa$|^PadAa$
column11: The substrate-binding subunit of phthalate 3,4-dioxygenase, required by KEGG module M00636. The token exists because the catalogue holds only the beta subunit of this enzyme. The veto words keep the route-1 enzyme, the beta subunit and the reductase out.

column3: phtAb@phthalate conversion to protocatechuic acid route 2
column8: \bphthalate 3,4-dioxygenase.{0,30}(beta|small)|\bphthalate dioxygenase.{0,15}(beta|small) subunit|small subunit of phthalate dioxygenase|^PhtAb$|^PadAb$
column11: The reference (A0A4R2Q9Z7, Tamaricihabitans halophyticus, TrEMBL, not curated, inferred from homology) is a ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase beta subunit, a broad family, so s_alone is false.

column3: phtAd@phthalate conversion to protocatechuic acid route 2
column8: \bphthalate 3,4-dioxygenase.{0,30}reductase|ferredoxin reductase of phthalate dioxygenase|^phthalate dioxygenase reductase subunit$|^PhtAd$
column11: The reference (Q0RWD0, Rhodococcus jostii RHA1 PadAd, TrEMBL, not curated) is a glutathione-reductase-type ferredoxin reductase, a large family, so s_alone is false. Supporting only, because KEGG M00636 marks the ferredoxin and reductase as optional.

column2: phthalate 3,4-cis-dihydrodiol dehydrogenase (short-chain dehydrogenase in Rhodococcus, Terrabacter and Mycobacterium; aldo-keto reductase in Arthrobacter keyseri)
column3: phtB@phthalate conversion to protocatechuic acid route 2
column11: The reference (A1T2B3, Mycolicibacterium vanbaalenii PYR-1, TrEMBL, not curated) is a short-chain dehydrogenase, whereas the Arthrobacter keyseri PhtB is an aldo-keto reductase (Pfam PF00248), so neither one structure nor one name covers both. That is why phtB is supporting only.

column3: phtC@phthalate conversion to protocatechuic acid route 2
column11: The reference (Q9AGK2) is the Swiss-Prot Arthrobacter keyseri enzyme, with protein-level evidence. Class II aldolase fold (about 52,000 proteins in InterPro, including fuculose-phosphate aldolase and ribulose-phosphate epimerase), so s_alone is false. Left out of the co-localised group because in Mycolicibacterium vanbaalenii PYR-1 the only decarboxylase KEGG assigns sits about 80 genes from the dioxygenase.

column2: beta-propeller phytase (BPP class: Bacillus PhyC type; calcium-dependent, active at neutral pH); also any phytase whose name does not state its class
column11: Beta-propeller phytase class (BPP: Bacillus PhyC/Phy; Pfam PF02333), the main phytase class of soil and water bacteria (Lim et al. 2007); needs calcium and works at neutral pH (Kerovuo et al. 1998). A structure hit alone does not count, because related beta-propellers exist. Bakta's plain names 'phytase' and '3-phytase' do not state the class and are read here, so this gene line means 'BPP, or a phytase whose name gives no class'; when such a protein also carries the HAP KO K01093 or EC 3.1.3.26 it shows under appA as well. 'Phytase domain' names are BPP-family proteins (for example a 640-aa PF02333 protein in Pseudomonas protegens Pf-5), often next to a TonB-dependent receptor, the arrangement Lim et al. (2007) describe for BPP genes.

Supporting only: PmsA is the histidine decarboxylase of the cluster, which supplies the histamine that PmsD attaches, and the protein is reviewed in UniProt as a histidine decarboxylase (Q1IAK7, gene hdc), while the symbol pmsA for the same locus comes from KEGG. The generic 'histidine decarboxylase' product and its orthologue number are deliberately NOT used, because that enzyme is common in food-associated bacteria and has nothing to do with siderophores; only the pseudomonine names count, so this token reports the gene where the cluster is annotated and stays silent otherwise.

Not in EcoFoldDB. The pyochelin orthologue number for this step is used on the pchB token instead, so that one protein is not counted under two systems; here only names with the letter name PmsB or PsmB count; the pathway name alone is in the PmsD and PmsE names and does not count. The alternative spelling psmB is accepted because the sequenced producer's annotation uses it for this gene, and the protein is small (about 105 residues) and annotated either 'isochorismate pyruvate-lyase' or 'chorismate mutase' depending on the genome.

Not in EcoFoldDB. Kept deliberately narrow: the generic 'isochorismate synthase' is the menaquinone enzyme MenF in nearly every genome, so only names with the letter name PmsC count; the pathway name alone is in the PmsD and PmsE names and does not count. In the sequenced producer this gene sits immediately next to pmsD.

UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the reviewed Pseudomonas entomophila PmsD, whose three activities (threonine loading, salicyl transfer and cyclisation, then transfer of N-hydroxyhistamine) were established in vitro; the same entry carries basA as a synonym, which is why that symbol is accepted. The orthologue number listed for this entry in the catalogue is the vibriobactin synthetase VibF, so it is deliberately not used as a matching route. Structure alone is not accepted: large NRPS proteins of other systems can pass the published thresholds against this entry, among them proteins that tie between the mycobactin and bacillibactin entries. The pathway name 'pseudomonine' does not count on its own: it is also in the name of PmsE.

PmsE is the better partner for pmsD than the two chorismate enzymes: it is the salicyl-AMP ligase of this pathway, reviewed in UniProt, and in the reconstituted system it hands the salicyl group to PmsD. Not in EcoFoldDB. The enzyme number EC 6.2.1.61 is shared with one other named enzyme, PchD of pyochelin, so the pyochelin names are vetoed here and the pseudomonine names on the pchD entry, which keeps one protein from being counted under two systems. The mycobactin and yersiniabactin ligases do the same chemistry under other, incomplete numbers, so their names are vetoed here too. The pathway name 'pseudomonine' does not count on its own: it is also in the name of PmsD.

Reference: p-hydroxybenzoate hydroxylase of Pseudomonas fluorescens (P00438, reviewed, evidence at protein level). Supporting only: it marks the 4-hydroxybenzoate funnel into protocatechuate, useful beside both protocatechuate rules and the toluene-4-monooxygenase rule. Flavin monooxygenase fold, so s_alone is false.

column2: PQQ precursor peptide PqqA (very short; often not called as a gene)
column8: \bPqqA\b|coenzyme PQQ synthesis protein A|pyrroloquinoline quinone precursor peptide
column11: Supporting: the precursor peptide (about 23 amino acids) that becomes PQQ; often missed by gene calling, so it is not required.
PQQ synthesis (pqqABCDE operon); not in EcoFoldDB, names only. PqqE names are vetoed, because PqqE proteins can carry the PqqB KO.

column2: pyrroloquinoline-quinone synthase PqqC (last step of PQQ synthesis)
column8: pyrroloquinoline[- ]quinone synthase|\bPqqC\b|coenzyme PQQ synthesis protein C|\bPqqC/?D\b
column11: Last step of PQQ synthesis; the marker used for phosphate-solubilising pseudomonads (Meyer et al. 2011). The symbol pqqC also lands on TenA / thiaminase-II proteins, which share the fold, so the symbol needs a PqqC name or KO. In four Methylobacterium species pqqC and pqqD are one fused gene (Shen et al. 2012); a fused C/D name counts for both pqqC and pqqD. Names that say PqqD are vetoed, because PqqD proteins can carry the PqqC KO and EC; the fused C/D names do not contain the word PqqD and still count.

column8: pyrroloquinoline quinone biosynthesis (peptide chaperone|protein) PqqD|coenzyme PQQ synthesis protein D|coenzyme PQQ synthesis protein C/D|\bPqqC/?D\b
column11: Peptide chaperone of PQQ synthesis, obligatory for PQQ production (Shen et al. 2012). Many ribosomal-peptide (RiPP) gene clusters have PqqD-like chaperones that Bakta names 'PqqD family' or 'lasso peptide biosynthesis PqqD family chaperone'; those are excluded and the symbol needs a real PqqD name. A fused PqqC/D (Methylobacterium) counts here when its name says C/D; when it is named only 'PqqC' (RefSeq), pqqD shows as missing and the trait as partial.

column2: PQQ biosynthesis radical SAM enzyme PqqE (PqqA peptide cyclase)
column8: \bPqqE\b|PqqA peptide cyclase|coenzyme PQQ synthesis protein E
column11: Radical SAM enzyme that links two residues of the PqqA peptide, the first step of PQQ synthesis.
Supporting: M16-family protease of PQQ synthesis; PqqL, a different M16 protease, is excluded.

Reference: PraC of Paenibacillus sp. JJ-1b (C4TP07), an unreviewed UniProt entry; in that strain it is the 4-oxalocrotonate tautomerase of the protocatechuate 2,3-cleavage operon (Kasai et al. 2009), not of a catechol pathway. Escherichia coli PptA is a phenylpyruvate tautomerase (P31992) and Bacillus subtilis YwhB a stand-alone 2-hydroxymuconate tautomerase (P70994), both reviewed; this is why the symbol pptA is not accepted and why this gene is supporting only and never counts from structure alone. xylH is the TOL symbol for this gene and the xylose permease symbol in Bakta.

The same enzyme as AlcA of alcaligin, which is why the alcaligin name is vetoed here: where the annotation says alcaligin, the gene should be counted under that system. No orthologue or enzyme route is used, both being shared across the whole putrescine, cadaverine and lysine N-hydroxylase family. UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the reviewed Shewanella oneidensis PubA, whose function rests on heterologous expression that produced free N-hydroxyputrescine. Structure alone is not accepted: a genome's own ornithine N5-monooxygenase can be the best-scoring protein against this entry. The pathway name 'putrebactin' does not count here: it is in the names of PubC and of the ferric putrebactin reductase.

Identical in function to AlcB of alcaligin, and the pathway-specific orthologue number for the putrebactin acyltransferase is listed. The catalogue entry's accession has been deleted from UniProtKB; the archived record shows a Shewanella MbtK/IucB-like 'Siderophore biosynthesis protein, putative' immediately beside the pubC gene, and the orthologous gene in the Shewanella oneidensis type strain is named 'N-hydroxyputrescine-succinyl CoA transferase PubB' - which is where the hydroxyputrescine name form comes from. The pathway name 'putrebactin' does not count here: it is in the names of PubC and of the ferric putrebactin reductase.

The ring-closing step, shown with purified enzyme to dimerise and macrocyclise N-hydroxy-N-succinylputrescine; UniProt's reviewed entry carries that function and the putrebactin synthase enzyme number, which is specific and is kept, along with the pathway-specific orthologue number. The fold is not specific, being the NRPS-independent siderophore synthetase family, so structure alone is not accepted. Bisucaberin and avaroferrin come from the same enzyme acting on cadaverine or on a mixed pair, which the rule's caveat states. 'Putrebactin' counts only as part of the synthase name; on its own it is also in the names of the reductase and the receptor.

Supporting only. Neither the orthologue number (K10531) nor the enzyme number (EC 1.14.13.195) for ornithine N5-monooxygenase is used: both also sit on other members of the family, such as Streptomyces MbtG proteins, lysine 6-monooxygenases and family-level proteins. Both routes are family-level, so only the product name counts.
Supporting only, and not in EcoFoldDB. The formylation of hydroxyornithine is specific to pyoverdine, so the name is reliable where the annotation provides it.

Supporting only. This is the same enzyme as EctB of ectoine synthesis and RhbA of rhizobactin synthesis, sharing their orthologue and enzyme numbers, which is why neither is used here and only the explicit PvdH name counts. Any protein matching pvdH will also match rhbA, by design: the rules, not the gene table, keep the two traits apart.

Not in EcoFoldDB, so this gene comes from the sequence name alone. It is the alternative to pvdQ in the required set, for strains whose PvdQ the annotation leaves unnamed. It is kept out of the co-localisation group because in the reference clusters pvdL sits 28 to 29 genes from pvdO, well beyond a 10-gene chain. The enzyme number the annotation attaches to it (a tRNA ligase number) is plainly wrong for this protein and is not used.

column8: pyoverdine biosynthesis protein PvdO|dihydropyoverdine dehydrogenase|pyoverdine chromophore maturation
column11: One of only two genes in this group where a structure hit alone counts, because the match is clean and the step is specific to pyoverdine. The generic family name 'SUMF1/EgtB/PvdO family nonheme iron enzyme' also sits on proteins of other genera that are not PvdO, so the pattern deliberately does not match it; those proteins are not counted rather than vetoed, since a veto would also throw away a genuine PvdO named that way. UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the P. aeruginosa PvdO and that it carries the FGE-sulfatase (SUMF) domain, the very fold those family-named proteins share, so a structure hit in another genus is possible. That is tolerable only because the rule also requires pvdP and their co-localisation: a lone spurious pvdO is one gene of three and cannot even reach partial.

The second gene allowed to count on structure alone, and the most specific structure in the group: PvdP is the tyrosinase that forms the chromophore, shown by mutant work and by in vitro oxidation of ferribactin. The pattern deliberately does not accept the ambiguous annotation 'PvdJ/PvdD/PvdP-like protein', which sits on proteins of other genera that may equally be the NRPS modules PvdJ or PvdD; a protein named that way therefore gives structure-only evidence rather than false sequence agreement.

column8: acyl-?homoserine lactone (acylase|deacylase) PvdQ|acyl-?homoserine lactone deacylase|ferribactin acylase
column11: Structure alone is not enough: besides the real PvdQ, penicillin amidases and the quorum-quenching acylase QuiP can take this entry as a passing hit. The orthologue and enzyme numbers are shared with QuiP and are not used. 'Penicillin' is deliberately not vetoed: PvdQ belongs to the penicillin acylase family, so a genuine PvdQ can legitimately be annotated 'Penicillin amidase', and vetoing that word would hide a true structure hit; a protein that carries the pvdQ symbol with only a penicillin name is kept out by the symbol gating. QuiP, HacB and aculeacin acylase names are vetoed, being different enzymes with the same fold.

The single clearest case of a shared enzyme in the group. This protein is also EctB of ectoine synthesis and PvdH of pyoverdine synthesis, with the same orthologue number, the same enzyme number and the same product name, so no pattern can separate them and none is attempted. The orthologue and enzyme routes are kept because the enzyme really is this one; what prevents harm is the rule, which requires all six rhizobactin genes together. UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the reviewed Sinorhizobium meliloti RhbA. Structure alone is firmly ruled out: many proteins of a single genome can pass the published thresholds against this entry, and some survive the best-hit filter. The pathway names 'rhizobactin' and 'schizokinen' do not count on their own: the transporters, the receptor and the regulator RhrA carry them too. A structure title of the decarboxylase domain of the fused transaminase-decarboxylase ('decarboxylase domain of diaminobutyrate-pyruvate transaminase and ...') is vetoed: it describes the decarboxylase part only.

The ddc symbol is accepted because it is the usual name for this enzyme, which also makes 1,3-diaminopropane outside siderophore synthesis; UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the reviewed Sinorhizobium RhbB. The annotation can put the gadA symbol on this enzyme, a reminder not to read a symbol on its own: here the product name is the reliable part. Structure alone is not accepted, the fold being a common pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase. The pathway names 'rhizobactin' and 'schizokinen' do not count on their own: the transporters, the receptor and the regulator RhrA carry them too.

A synthetase of the NRPS-independent siderophore family, so structure alone is not accepted; UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the reviewed Sinorhizobium RhbC with IucA/IucC domains. The chemical name of the reaction is accepted too, because the annotation sometimes uses it in place of the gene name. The pathway names 'rhizobactin' and 'schizokinen' do not count on their own: the transporters (RhtX, SchT, SchE), the receptor and the regulator RhrA carry them too, so one such protein would otherwise stand for every gene of the cluster.

A small acetyltransferase of the same family as DesC, AlcB, PubB and IucB, so structure alone is not accepted. UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the reviewed Sinorhizobium RhbD; the pathway-specific orthologue number is listed. The pathway names 'rhizobactin' and 'schizokinen' do not count on their own: the transporters, the receptor and the regulator RhrA carry them too.

Shares the orthologue number of the putrescine, cadaverine and diaminopropane N-hydroxylase family with AlcA, PubA and DesB, so no orthologue route is used. UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the reviewed Sinorhizobium RhbE of that flavin-dependent hydroxylase family. Structure alone is not accepted: other proteins, such as a genome's PvdA or a flavorubredoxin reductase, can pass the published thresholds against this entry. The pathway names 'rhizobactin' and 'schizokinen' do not count on their own: the transporters, the receptor and the regulator RhrA carry them too. In Bakta's database the cluster of the Sinorhizobium RhbE itself (Swiss-Prot Q9Z3Q8) is named 'putative histamine N-monooxygenase', so that name counts too. The same name is given to the histamine N-hydroxylases of other siderophores, such as acinetobactin and anguibactin, which is why a call needs all six genes together and a partial needs rhbC, rhbD or rhbF: those three are recognised only by names and orthologue numbers of this cluster, whereas rhbA, rhbB and this hydroxylase are shared with other pathways.

The core synthase of the pathway, again a member of the NRPS-independent siderophore synthetase family, so structure alone is not accepted; UniProt confirms the catalogue entry is the reviewed Sinorhizobium RhbF. The orthologue number the curated orthology gives this step is named 'schizokinen synthase', which is the clearest single piece of evidence that these six genes cannot distinguish rhizobactin 1021 from schizokinen - hence the rule's caveat. By name only RhbF counts, and RhsF, the second gene name UniProt gives this protein, when the name also says rhizobactin; the pathway names alone do not count, because the transporters, the receptor and the regulator carry them too.

column2: arginine decarboxylase (biosynthetic SpeA; the acid-induced AdiA also counts)
column11: Both arginine decarboxylases make agmatine, the substrate of speB or aguA. EcoFoldDB's speA structure (UniProt Q8ZHG8, the 659-aa biosynthetic enzyme of Yersinia pestis) is large and distinct from the shorter diaminopimelate decarboxylases in the background, so a structure hit counts alone. AdiA belongs to another family and is found by name.

Bakta gives the name 'agmatinase' also to arginase-family enzymes that carry a guanidinobutyrase or guanidinopropionase KO (K12255, K18459, K25365) and two or three EC numbers instead of EC 3.5.3.11 alone, for example in Pseudomonas and Arthrobacter. The name cannot separate these arginase-family enzymes, so the speA+speB route can be satisfied by a misnamed guanidinobutyrase; this matters little because putrescine synthesis is near-universal (see the rule caveat). EcoFoldDB's background holds guanidinobutyrases and arginases, so a structure hit to speB (UniProt P70999, Bacillus subtilis) counts alone.

EcoFoldDB's speC structure is E. coli SpeF (UniProt P24169), a fold-type I decarboxylase. EcoFoldDB's background lacks the lysine decarboxylases CadA and LdcC and the biodegradative arginine decarboxylase AdiA of the same family, so these can best-match it: structure alone is not enough. Fold-type III ornithine decarboxylases are too short to pass the coverage filter against SpeF and are found by name.

column2: S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase (SpeD; called SpeH in Bacillus)
column11: One token covers EcoFoldDB's speD and speH structures, the same enzyme under two gene names. They cover both size classes: Bacillus licheniformis SpeH (UniProt Q65G98, 128 aa) is the short type of Firmicutes and archaea, and Desulfitobacterium hafniense SpeD (UniProt B8G177, 276 aa) the longer type, 62% identical to E. coli SpeD.
Spermidine synthase needs decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine from speD, or the strain uses the aspartate-semialdehyde route instead (cansdh + nspC).

column2: toluene monooxygenase, hydroxylase alpha subunit (diiron active site)
column11: Reference protein UniProt Q00456, reviewed, Ectopseudomonas (Pseudomonas) mendocina, protein-level evidence. The bare product 'Toluene hydroxylase' is vetoed in every tmo entry, because Bakta also gives that name to proteins with no connection to toluene, among them genes inside prophages. No EC listed because all four hydroxylase subunits share 1.14.13.236. The alternative symbols are the toluene-3-monooxygenase subunit tbuA1 and the toluene/o-xylene monooxygenase subunit touA, which UniProt names as the alpha hydroxylase subunits of their systems.
Reference protein UniProt Q00457, reviewed, E. mendocina. UniProt names tbuU the gamma hydroxylase subunit of the toluene-3-monooxygenase, which is why it is the alternative symbol here.

Reference protein UniProt Q00458, reviewed, E. mendocina. A Rieske ferredoxin, the least specific fold of the complex, and KEGG also maps its KO to sulfur metabolism. KEGG marks this component non-essential in its module; it is kept required here because the mutagenesis work on the reference cluster found each of the five genes essential for activity.

Reference protein UniProt Q00459, reviewed, E. mendocina. The effector protein that sets which ring position is attacked; small and poorly conserved, so it depends on the name. 'Activator' is accepted as well, since UniProt uses that word for the homologue tbuV. Ferredoxin names are vetoed, because a ferredoxin can carry 'effector protein' in its name.
Reference protein UniProt Q00460, reviewed, E. mendocina. Shares the diiron fold with the methane monooxygenase subunits, which carry names of their own such as 'Methane monooxygenase component C'.

Reference protein UniProt Q03304, reviewed, E. mendocina. Supporting rather than required: it raises activity of the five-gene complex two- to threefold and the naphthalene dioxygenase reductase can largely replace it, so a cluster whose reductase Bakta names generically must not be downgraded to partial. A generic flavin reductase outside its operon context, hence s_alone false.

The reference (Q3C1E0) is the Swiss-Prot Comamonas sp. E6 TphA1. A ferredoxin-NADP reductase-type flavoprotein with a ferredoxin domain, like the reductases of many other oxygenases and of dideoxy-sugar synthesis, so a structure hit never counts alone.

The reference (Q3C1E3) is the Swiss-Prot Comamonas sp. E6 TphA2, with protein-level evidence: the substrate-binding subunit. EC 1.14.12.15 is left out of all three dioxygenase components because the catalogue gives it to each. A Rieske oxygenase, so s_alone is false.
The reference (Q3C1E2) is the Swiss-Prot Comamonas sp. E6 TphA3. Its fold (NTF2-like) belongs to a very large superfamily, so s_alone is false.

The reference (Q3C1E1) is the Swiss-Prot Comamonas sp. E6 TphB. PdxA family (InterPro IPR005255), whose vitamin B6 enzyme PdxA is common in Proteobacteria, so s_alone is false. Do not add EC 1.1.1.262: one Rhodococcus entry carries it, but it is the PdxA number.

Not in EcoFoldDB's catalogue. TreS interconverts maltose and trehalose in the test tube (De Smet et al. 2000). On its own it has not been shown to make trehalose in a living cell: in Pseudomonas syringae both loci were needed, since deleting either the treS locus or the treY/treZ locus stopped trehalose accumulating (Freeman et al. 2010), and in many bacteria TreS instead feeds trehalose into alpha-glucan through the GlgE pathway (Chandra et al. 2011). That is why it is reported as supporting evidence and does not make a call by itself. In Pseudomonas TreS is often fused to maltokinase, and Bakta then sometimes names the whole protein 'Maltokinase', which this entry misses.
Works with treZ on malto-oligosaccharides from glycogen; the two usually sit together with glgX and malQ (De Smet et al. 2000).
A GH13 enzyme, like glycogen debranching enzyme GlgX and TreS. The borderline flag marks near-ties with them.

column2: urease gamma subunit (in Helicobacter fused with the beta subunit)
column8: urease (subunit )?gamma|urease gamma subunit|urease,? (subunit )?(gamma/beta|beta/gamma)|fusion of urease (beta and gamma|gamma and beta)
column11: Small gamma subunit. In many bacteria (Helicobacter, Bradyrhizobium, Pseudomonas syringae, Methylobacterium, Streptomyces) the gamma and beta subunits are one fused protein (KEGG K14048, 'ureAB'); RefSeq usually names it after one subunit only ('urease subunit gamma' or 'urease subunit beta'), which is why the rule needs ureC plus either small subunit. K14048 and fused names count for both ureA and ureB. Helicobacter names are swapped (the fused small protein is 'urease subunit alpha', the large catalytic one 'urease subunit beta'), so its gene lines can show crossed names while the call is still right.

column2: urease beta subunit (in Helicobacter fused with the gamma subunit)
column8: urease (subunit )?beta|urease beta subunit|urease,? (subunit )?(gamma/beta|beta/gamma)|fusion of urease (beta and gamma|gamma and beta)
column11: Small beta subunit; often fused with gamma (KEGG K14048, which counts here too; see ureA). The structure hit of a plain UreB is weak because the protein is small (about 100-160 amino acids). In Helicobacter the large catalytic subunit carries the name ureB / 'urease subunit beta', so it also lands here; the decision is unaffected.

column2: urease alpha subunit (catalytic, nickel active site)
column11: Large catalytic alpha subunit with the nickel active site; the strongest structure evidence of the three. KEGG K01427 (single-chain urease) is accepted because Bakta sometimes puts it on bacterial UreC. A bare 'urease' name is not used, because in bacteria it can label the fused small subunit.

column2: urease accessory protein UreD (called UreH in Helicobacter)
column11: Supporting; called UreH in Helicobacter. Bakta's 'Urease accessory protein UreH-like transmembrane domain-containing protein' is an unrelated membrane-protein family (DsbD-like) and is excluded.
Supporting; carries nickel to the active site.
Supporting; part of the UreD-UreF-UreG activation complex.
Supporting; GTPase that inserts nickel. The generic HypB-like 'Ni2+-binding GTPase involved in ... urease and hydrogenase' is not matched.

column8: vanadium-iron protein,? alpha|vanadium-dependent nitrogenase,? alpha|V-containing nitrogenase,? (subunit )?alpha|\bVnfD\b
column11: Supporting only. The EcoFoldDB structure is an Anabaena variabilis VnfD fused to VnfG. A structure hit alone does not count, because the alpha chains of the three nitrogenases look alike; the vanadium name or KO must be present.

column2: vanadium nitrogenase, delta chain (no counterpart in the molybdenum nitrogenase)
column8: vanadium-iron protein,? delta|vanadium nitrogenase,? delta|V-containing nitrogenase,? (subunit )?delta|\bVnfG\b
column11: Supporting only. The delta subunit exists only in the alternative nitrogenases, so it is the clearest sign of one. EcoFoldDB labels this entry 'reductase component', but its structure (UniProt P16857) is the VnfG delta chain.

column8: vanadium-iron protein,? beta|vanadium-dependent nitrogenase,? beta|V-containing nitrogenase,? (subunit )?beta|\bVnfK\b
column11: Supporting only; a structure hit alone does not count (the beta chains of the three nitrogenases look alike).

column2: xylene/toluene methyl-monooxygenase, electron transfer component XylA
column8: xylene.{0,20}monooxygenase.{0,40}electron transfer|xylene monooxygenase.{0,30}reductase|toluene methyl-monooxygenase electron transfer
column11: Reference protein UniProt P21394, reviewed, P. putida TOL plasmid. The token is spelt xylA_tol so that the rules table cannot be misread as carrying the xylose-isomerase gene; the EcoFoldDB key keeps the catalogue's own name xylA, and the catalogue holds three unrelated xylA entries under hemicellulose degradation. XylA is one protein with two domains, a chloroplast-type ferredoxin and a ferredoxin-NAD(P) reductase, so on its own it is an ordinary electron-transfer protein.

column2: aryl-alcohol (benzyl alcohol) dehydrogenase; the TOL XylB belongs to this activity group
column11: Reference protein UniProt P39849, reviewed, P. putida TOL plasmid. Every route for this gene is group-level evidence: ExPASy calls EC 1.1.1.90 a group of enzymes with broad specificity for aromatic primary alcohols, and KEGG's K00055 has no gene symbol at all. So a match says the strain has a benzyl-alcohol-type dehydrogenase, not that it has the TOL gene, and the gene is supporting only and never required. The wording 'benzyl alcohol dehydrogenase' is not accepted, because Bakta gives that exact name mostly to glutathione-dependent formaldehyde dehydrogenases (FrmA).

column2: benzaldehyde dehydrogenase (NAD+) of the TOL upper pathway
column11: Reference protein UniProt P43503, reviewed, P. putida TOL plasmid. Unlike xylB, this gene's KO (K00141) carries the gene symbol xylC and EC 1.2.1.28 is a single defined reaction, so the evidence is gene-level; it is still supporting only, because the benzaldehyde dehydrogenase step is shared with other routes to benzoate.

Reference protein UniProt P21395, reviewed, Pseudomonas putida TOL plasmid, protein-level evidence. XylM is an integral-membrane diiron hydroxylase about 25 percent identical to the alkane hydroxylase AlkB, which is common in Pseudomonas, so a structure hit alone cannot name it. Every xyl entry vetoes xylose and xylulose names, the collision to guard against in this group. The KEGG wording 'toluene methyl-monooxygenase' is accepted as well.
